(p-220) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Nisa'

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And give the orphans their property﴾, and so on. In this noble verse Allah, exalted is He, commands that the orphans be given their property, and He did not stipulate any condition here. However, He clarified elsewhere that this giving commanded is conditional upon two conditions:

The first: the orphans reaching maturity (bulugh).

The second: the sensing of maturity of judgment (rushd) in them. This is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And test the orphans until they reach marriageable age. Then if you perceive in them sound judgment, release to them their property﴾ [An-Nisa: 6].

Their being called "orphans" in both places is only by consideration of the orphanhood they had characterized by before reaching maturity, since there is no orphanhood after maturity by consensus (ijma'). A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the magicians were thrown down prostrating﴾ [Al-A'raf: 120], meaning those who had been magicians, since there is no magic with prostration to Allah.

Some scholars said: the meaning of giving them their property is the provision of maintenance and clothing during the period of guardianship over them.

Abu Hanifa said: when he reaches twenty-five years of age, his property is given to him in all circumstances, because he then becomes mature (jidd). The lack of soundness of this view is not hidden, and Allah knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not consume their property in addition to your own property. Indeed, that is ever a great sin (hububan kabiran)﴾. In this noble verse He mentions that consuming the property of orphans is a great sin (hubub), that is, a great offense. He did not explain the extent of the greatness of this sin, but He explained it in another place, which is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly are only consuming fire into their bellies, and they will burn in a Blaze﴾ [An-Nisa: 10].

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 3:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphan girls, then marry from among the women what pleases you﴾

The verse. It is not hidden what comes to mind regarding this noble verse: the connection between this condition and this consequence is not apparent. Accordingly, there is a degree of ambiguity (ijmal) in the verse. The meaning, as Umm al-Mu'minin 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said, is that a man would have an orphan girl in his guardianship (hijr). If she was beautiful, he would marry her without being just regarding her bridal gift (sadaq). If she was plain, he would dislike marrying her and would prevent her from marrying anyone else, so that he would not have to share her wealth. So they were forbidden to marry them unless they acted justly toward them and gave them the highest customary bridal gift (sunnat al-sadaq) for their kind. They were commanded to marry other women of their choosing instead. That is, just as he would dislike marrying her if she had little wealth and camels, it is not lawful for him to marry her if she has wealth and camels except by acting justly toward her and fulfilling her rights completely, without any deficiency. This meaning that Umm al-Mu'minin 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, adopted is clarified and supported by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They ask you concerning women. Say, "Allah gives you a ruling concerning them, and what is recited to you in the Book concerning the orphan girls to whom you do not give what is prescribed for them and whom you desire to marry"﴾ [An-Nisa': 127]. 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, also said: the intended meaning of "what is recited to you in the Book" is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphan girls﴾, etc. This shows that they are orphan women, as is evidenced by His explicit statement in the saying: ﴿orphan women to whom you do not give what is prescribed for them﴾, etc. From this it becomes clear that the meaning is: "And if you fear that you will not act justly in marrying orphan girls, then leave them, and marry from among the women other than them what pleases you." The response to the condition is a clear proof of this, because the connection between the condition and the consequence requires it. This is the most apparent of the opinions, due to the indication of the Qur'an. Accordingly, yatama is the plural of yatima (orphan girl) in an inverted form (qalb), as it was said: ayama (plural of ayyim, widow), and the original form was ayaʾim and yataʾim, since it is known that the plural of fa'ila (feminine form) is fa'a'il. This inversion is regular in words with a weak final radical, such as qadiyya, matiyya, and similar words, and it is restricted to what is transmitted (samaʿ) in other cases.

Ibn Khuwayz Mandad said: From this verse is derived the permissibility of a guardian (wasi) buying from and selling to himself from the orphan's property without favoritism, and the ruler (sultan) has the authority to review whatever occurs of that.

Some scholars derived from this verse that if the guardian (wali) wishes to marry the one under his guardianship, it is permissible for him to be both the one marrying and the one giving in marriage. This was the position of Malik, Abu Hanifa, al-Awza'i, al-Thawri, and Abu Thawr, and it was said by the Successors Hasan and Rabi'a, and it is the view of al-Layth.

Zufar and al-Shafi'i said: it is not permissible for him to marry her except with the permission of the ruler, or unless another guardian closer to her or equal to him marries her.

Ahmad said in one of the two narrations: he appoints another man as his agent so that he marries her to him. This was narrated from al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba, as al-Qurtubi and others transmitted.

Malik ibn Anas took from 'A'isha's explanation of this verse, as we have mentioned, the return to the customary bridal gift (sadaq al-mithl) in cases where the bridal gift is invalid, or where there has been a deception (ghabn) in its amount. This is because 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "and give them the highest customary bridal gift for them," which indicates that there is a known customary bridal gift for each class of people according to their circumstances. Malik said: "People have marriage customs known to them, and they recognize them," meaning bridal gifts and suitable matches (akfa').

It is also derived from this verse that it is permissible to marry an orphan girl if her rights are given to her in full. As for what many scholars said, that an orphan girl may not be married until she reaches puberty, arguing that the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They ask you concerning women﴾ is a term that applies to adult women and not to young girls, this is clearly invalid, because Allah explicitly stated that they are orphans, by the saying: ﴿concerning the orphan women﴾. This term may also be applied to young girls, as in the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They slaughter your sons and keep your women alive﴾ [Al-Baqara: 49], and they were then infants. The apparent and immediate meaning of the verse is the permissibility of marrying an orphan girl with fairness regarding the bridal gift and other rights.

The Sunnah indicates that she is not to be compelled, so she is not to be married except with her consent, even though a great many scholars disagreed regarding her marriage.

A note

Al-Qurtubi said in his tafsir of this verse, and his words are: "All who engage in the sciences agree that the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphan girls﴾ does not have a mafhum (implicit meaning by implication). For the Muslims have reached consensus (ijma') that whoever does not fear injustice regarding orphans may marry more than one wife: two, or three, or four, just as one who does fear may. This indicates that the verse was revealed in answer to one who feared that, and its ruling is more general than that." End of his quoted words.

The one who ascribes this commentary (muqayyid), may Allah pardon him, says: What appears in the verse according to what 'A'isha explained it, which al-Qurtubi and many verifying scholars accepted, and which the Qur'an indicates, is that it does have a valid mafhum. Its meaning is: "And if you fear that you will not act justly toward the orphan women, then marry from among others what pleases you." Its mafhum is that if they do not fear injustice, they are not commanded to go beyond them to others. Rather, it is permissible for them, in that case, to limit themselves to them. This is clear, as you see. However, when Allah commanded them to go beyond them to others upon fearing that they would not act justly toward them, He pointed to the permissible amount of plurality of wives. There is no difficulty in this, and Allah knows best.

Some scholars said: the meaning of the verse ﴿And if you fear that you will not act justly with the orphan girls﴾ is: if you fear this and are scrupulous about wronging orphans, then also fear and be scrupulous about wronging women by not treating them justly and by not fulfilling their rights. So reduce the number of wives you marry and do not exceed four. If you fear that it is not possible to do this with plurality, then limit yourselves to one wife, because a woman is similar to an orphan, since each of them is weak and unable to defend their right. Just as you feared wronging her, fear wronging her too.

Some scholars said: they used to be scrupulous about guardianship of orphans but were not scrupulous about adultery (zina). So it was said to them in the verse: If you fear sin regarding the property of the orphan, then fear the sin of adultery. So marry what pleases you of women and do not approach adultery. This is the most remote of the opinions, as it appears, and Allah the Exalted knows best.

From this noble verse it is also derived that whoever has an orphan girl in his guardianship may not marry her except by fulfilling her rights completely. It is also permissible to marry four wives, and more than that is forbidden, as the consensus of the Muslims before the emergence of the deviant dissenter also indicates. The Prophet ﷺ said to Ghaylan ibn Salama: "Choose four of them and divorce the rest." Likewise he said to al-Harith ibn Qays al-Asadi. And with fear of not being just, it is not permissible to marry more than one. The word "fear" in the verse: some scholars said its meaning is apprehension (khashya), and some scholars said its meaning is knowledge, i.e., "And if you know that you will not act justly..." From the usage of "fear" in the sense of "knowledge" is the saying of Abu Mihjan al-Thaqafi [Tawil meter]:

When I die, bury me beside a vine whose roots water my bones in death.
And do not bury me in the wasteland, for indeed I fear, if I die, that I will not taste it.

So his saying "akhafu" (I fear) means "a'lamu" (I know).

A note

In this verse, Allah the Exalted referred to women with "ma," which is used for non-rational beings, in the saying: ﴿marry what pleases you﴾ [An-Nisa': 3], and He did not say "man" (who), because here what is intended is the attributes and not the essences. That is, "what pleases you of a virgin or a previously married woman," or "what pleases you because it is lawful." When the intended meaning is the attribute, the rational is referred to with "ma," as in your saying "ma Zayd?" in the interrogative, meaning "Are they excellent?"

Some scholars said: He referred to them with "ma" as an indication of their deficiency, and He likened them to what does not reason, since they are taken in exchange (for a dowry), and Allah the Exalted knows best.
