The author said in *Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab* (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction from the Verses of the Book):

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

Surah An-Nisa'

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if you fear that you will not be just, then [marry only] one﴾, etc.

This noble verse indicates that justice among wives is possible. Another verse indicates that it is not possible, which is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And you will never be able to be just between wives, even if you should strive to do so﴾, etc. [An-Nisa': 129].

The answer to this: the justice among them that Allah mentioned as possible is justice in fulfilling the legal rights. The justice that He mentioned as impossible is equality in love and natural inclination, because this is an emotional state (infi'al) and not an action (fi'l), so it is not within human capacity. The intended meaning is that whoever is naturally more inclined toward one of his wives should fear Allah and be just in the legal rights, as indicated by His saying: ﴿So do not incline completely [toward one], leaving the other as if suspended﴾, etc. [An-Nisa': 129].

This reconciliation (jam') was narrated in meaning from Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ubayda al-Salmani, Mujahid, al-Hasan al-Basri, and al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim. Ibn Kathir transmitted this from them in his tafsir of the saying: ﴿And you will never be able to be just between wives﴾, etc.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abi Mulayka that the verse ﴿And you will never be able to be just between wives﴾ was revealed concerning 'A'isha, because the Prophet ﷺ was naturally inclined to her more than to the others.

Imam Ahmad and the authors of the Sunan narrated from 'A'isha, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to divide [his time] among his wives and be just, then he would say: 'O Allah, this is my division in what I control, so do not blame me for what You control and I do not control,'" meaning the heart. Ended, from Ibn Kathir.

Allah's saying: ﴿For men is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, and for women is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave, whether it is little or much — an obligatory share﴾. Here He did not specify the measure of this share which belongs to men and women from what the parents and close relatives leave. But He specified it in the verses of inheritance, such as His saying: ﴿Allah instructs you concerning your children﴾ — the two verses [An-Nisa: 11] — and His saying at the end of this noble surah: ﴿They ask you for a legal decision. Say: Allah gives you a decision concerning the kalalah﴾ — the verse [An-Nisa: 176].

The words of Allah, "Allah instructs you concerning your children: for the male, what is equal to the share of two females" (ﷺ... ) [4:11], did not here explain the wisdom behind preferring the male over the female in inheritance, although they are equal in kinship. However, He pointed to that in another place, which is His saying: "Men are in charge of women by [right of] what Allah has given one over the other and what they spend from their wealth" [4:34]. The reason is that the one in charge who spends his wealth on another is always exposed to a decrease, while the one in charge of whom wealth is spent is always exposed to an increase. The wisdom in giving preference to the one exposed to decrease over the one exposed to increase, by way of compensating for the anticipated loss, is very evident.

The words of Allah, "And if there are [only] daughters, more than two, for them is two thirds of what he leaves; and if there is only one, for her is half" [4:11], explicitly state that if the daughters are three or more, they receive two thirds. His saying "more than two" gives the impression that two daughters are not in this case, and He explicitly states that a single daughter receives half, from which it is understood that two daughters are likewise not in this case. Accordingly, there is an ambiguity in the verse's indication of the amount of inheritance of two daughters.

Allah, exalted is He, has indicated in two places that this qualifier has no contrary implication (mafhum mukhalafa), and that two daughters also receive two thirds:

The first is His saying: "for the male, what is equal to the share of two females", since a male inherits two thirds alongside one female without dispute. Therefore there must be a case in which two daughters receive two thirds; otherwise "what is equal to the share of two females" would have no meaning, since two thirds is not a share for them at all. But that case is not a case of their combination, since there is no case in which two daughters combine with a male and receive two thirds. Thus it is necessarily the case of their being alone without a male. The objection of some to this argument, that it leads to circularity (dawr), saying that knowing that the male has two thirds in the stated case depends on knowing the share of the two females, because the verse only states that the male has what is equal to the share of two females, and that if the share of the two females were derived from the share of the male, circularity would result, is invalid. This is because what is derived is the specific share of the two females, which is two thirds, while what knowledge of the male's share depends on is knowledge of the share of the two females in general, so there is no circularity, since the aspects are distinct. Some have also objected that a son with two daughters receives half, which indicates that their prescribed share is half. What supports the first argument is that when the two daughters, together with a male, received half, it is known that if they were alone without him they would receive more than that, since a single daughter when alone takes half, whereas when with him she takes a third. What further clarifies this is that a daughter takes a third alongside a male son without dispute, so it is even more fitting that she take it alongside a female daughter.

Thus it becomes clear that He, majestic and exalted, indicated the inheritance of two daughters by His saying: "for the male, what is equal to the share of two females", as we have explained. Then He mentioned the ruling for a group of daughters and for a single one of them, by His saying: "And if there are [only] daughters, more than two, for them is two thirds of what he leaves; and if there is only one, for her is half." What further clarifies this is that He made it a consequence of the preceding by the particle fa' (therefore) in His saying: "fa-in kunna" (and if they are...), for if there were nothing before it indicating the portion of the females, the fa' would not fall in its proper place, as is evident.

The second place is His saying regarding two sisters: "And if they are two, then for them are two thirds of what he leaves" [4:176], because the daughter is closer in kinship and stronger in cause for inheritance than the sister, without dispute.

When Allah has explicitly stated that two sisters receive two thirds, it is known that two daughters are likewise entitled, by a fortiori reasoning. Most scholars hold that fahwa al-khitab, namely mafhum al-muwafaqa (the implication of agreement), in which the unmentioned case is more deserving of the ruling than the mentioned one, is from the category of the indication of the wording and not from the category of analogy (qiyas), contrary to al-Shafi'i and a group of others, as is known in the principles of jurisprudence. So when Allah, blessed and exalted, explained that two sisters receive two thirds, He thereby implied that two daughters are likewise entitled, a fortiori.

Likewise, when He explicitly stated that for daughters beyond two, the portion is two thirds only, and did not mention the ruling for sisters beyond two, He also implied, a fortiori, that sisters beyond two receive nothing other than two thirds. For since He did not give the daughters more than that, it is known that sisters are not entitled to more. So the unmentioned case in both matters is more deserving of the ruling than the mentioned one, and this is evidence that He intended to take it from that. What further clarifies what we have mentioned is what Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah related from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The wife of Sa'd ibn al-Rabi' came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, these are the two daughters of Sa'd, whose father was killed at Uhud, and their paternal uncle has taken their wealth and left them no wealth, and they cannot be married unless they have wealth.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Allah, the Exalted, will decide concerning that.' Then the verse of inheritance was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent for their uncle and said: 'Give the two daughters of Sa'd two thirds, give their mother one eighth, and what remains is yours.'"

As for what is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: the two daughters receive half, because Allah, exalted is He, said: "and if [they are] more than two, for them are two thirds of what he leaves", thereby explicitly stating that two thirds belong only to what is above two, this is refuted in several respects:

First: it is itself refuted by a like argument, because Allah also said: "and if there is only one, for her is half", explicitly stating that half is for a single one, making her being alone a condition upon which the prescription of half depends. It is established in the principles that when implications conflict, the stronger of them is given precedence, and it is known that the implication of a condition is stronger than the implication of a qualifier (zarf), because no other implication takes precedence over the implication of a condition except what some scholars have said is a statement rather than an implication, namely negation and affirmation and the forms of restriction and limit (ghaya). Other than these, the implication of a condition takes precedence. In Maraqi al-Su'ud, explaining the grades of the implication of contrariety, he said:

"Its highest is not guided except by the learned, and what is attributed to a statement is of weak standing.
So the condition, then the descriptive qualifier that is suitable, then the unrestricted descriptive qualifier which is near,
Then the number, there is a precedence that follows, and it is a proof upon the clear path."

The author of Jam' al-Jawami' said, in its text: "The question of the limit (ghaya) is said to be a statement, but the correct view is that it is an implication, followed by the condition, then the suitable qualifier, then the unrestricted qualifier other than number, then number, then the precedence of the object (taqdim al-ma'mul), etc."

From this you know that the implication of the condition in His saying: "and if she is one, for her is half" is stronger than the implication of the qualifier (zarf) in His saying: "fa-in kunna nisa'an fawqa thnatayn" (and if they are women above two).

Second: the indications of the preceding verses that two daughters receive two thirds.

Third: the explicit statement of the Prophet (ﷺ) to this effect in the hadith of Jabir mentioned just above.

Fourth: it is narrated from Ibn Abbas that he retracted that view.

Al-Alusi said in his Tafsir, in its text: "In Sharh al-Yanbu' it is quoted from al-Sharif Shams al-Din al-Armuni that he said in Sharh Fara'id al-Waseet: 'The retraction of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, on that is authentic, so it became a consensus (ijma').'" End of quotation in his words.

* *

Two reminders

First: what some scholars mentioned and Al-Alusi affirmed in his Tafsir, that the implication in His saying "and if she is one, for her is half" is an implication of number, is an error. The correct view is what we have mentioned, that it is an implication of condition, which is stronger than the implication of number by several degrees, as you have seen above.

In Nashr al-Bunud 'ala Maraqi al-Su'ud, in explaining his verse:

"It is the qualifier of cause or number, and from it is the condition or the limit that is relied upon."

it says: "The meaning of the implication of the condition is what is understood from attaching a ruling to something by a conditional particle such as 'in' (if) and 'idha' (when)." And in explaining this same verse, before this, it says: "Among them is the condition, such as His saying: 'And if they are pregnant, then spend upon them' [65:6], the implication being the negation of the conditioned when the condition is negated, i.e., those who are not pregnant are not obligated to be maintained; and such as: whoever purifies himself, his prayer is valid." End of quotation in his words.

Likewise His saying: "and if she is one, for her is half" attaches the prescription of half to a condition, which is that the daughter is one, and its implication is that if the condition, which is her being one, is negated, the conditioned, which is the prescription of half, is negated, as is evident. If it is said that the implication is likewise in His saying "fa-in kunna nisa'an fawqa thnatayn", since it is attached to a condition, the answer is in two respects:

First: the essence of the condition is their being women, and His saying "fawqa thnatayn" is an additional qualifier, while her being one is the condition itself, not an additional qualifier. You already know the precedence of the implication of the condition over the implication of the qualifier, whether zarf or otherwise.

Second: even if we grant, for the sake of argument, that it is an implication of condition, the two implications would cancel each other out, since they are equal, and the proof would be sought from outside. We have mentioned the proofs that two daughters inherit two thirds, as already mentioned.

Second: If it is said: what is the benefit of the expression "fawqa thnatayn" if two are already so entitled? The answer is in two respects:

First: it is what we mentioned, that the ruling for two was taken from His saying before it: "for the male, what is equal to the share of two females", as already mentioned; so His saying "fawqa thnatayn" is an explicit statement of the ruling for three and above, as already mentioned.

Second: the word "fawq" was mentioned to indicate that daughters do not receive more than two thirds, however many they may be.

As for the claim that the word "fawq" is superfluous, or that "fawqa thnatayn" means "two or more than them", all of this is clearly untenable, as you see, and the Qur'an is exalted above the like of it, even if a group of scholars has held it.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 12:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And if a man leaves neither parents nor children, and has a brother or a sister, then each of them shall have a sixth. But if they are more than that, they shall share in a third﴾. The intended meaning of "brothers" in this verse is the brothers whose single member takes a sixth, and when they are multiple they share the third, males and females alike. This is the brothers of the mother (uterine brothers), as evidenced by His explanation, may He be exalted, that brothers from the father, whether full or half, a single one of them inherits the entire estate, and when they are together they inherit the whole estate, with the male receiving the portion of two females.

He spoke of the single one among them, who inherits from her, if she has no child, and He said of their group: ﴿And if they are brothers and sisters, men and women, then the male receives the portion of two females﴾. The scholars have agreed that these brothers are from the mother, and whether they are full brothers or half-brothers from the father. Just as they agreed that His saying: ﴿And if a man leaves neither parents nor children (kalalah)﴾, the verse, refers to brothers of the mother. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas recited "and he has a brother or a sister from a mother." The verification is that the intended meaning of kalalah is the absence of ascendants and descendants, as the poet said:

"They ask you about kalalah; it is the cutting off of offspring without doubt.
No parent remains and no child; so the sons and grandfathers are cut off."

This is the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, and most of the Companions, and it is the truth, Allah willing. Know that kalalah is applied to kinship other than through child or parent, to a deceased who left neither parent nor child, to an heir who is neither parent nor child, and to property inherited from one who is neither parent nor child; however, this usage is not widespread. The derivation of kalalah has been disputed.

Many scholars chose that its origin is from "takallalahu" (it surrounded him), when it encircles him, and from it comes al-iklil (the crown), because it encircles the head, and al-kull (the whole) because of its encompassing of the number; for the heirs in this case surround the deceased from his sides, not from his ascendants or descendants.

Some scholars said: its origin is from al-kalal, meaning fatigue, because kalalah is weaker than kinship of parents and children.

Some scholars said: its origin is from al-kull, meaning the back, and accordingly it is what the deceased left behind his back. The grammatical analysis of His saying "kalalah" has been disputed. Some scholars said: it is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the deputy subject of "yuwarathu", with an omitted modifier, i.e., he is inherited from while being in the state of having kalalah, that is, kinship other than parents and children. Al-Zajjaj chose this, and it is the most apparent. It was also said: it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), i.e., he is inherited from for the sake of kalalah, that is, kinship. It was also said: it is the predicate of "kana", and "yuwarathu" is an attribute of "rajul," i.e., there was a man, an inherited one, having kalalah, neither parent nor child. It was also said other than that. And Allah, may He be exalted, knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 15:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness, bring against them four witnesses from among you; and if they testify, then confine them to the houses until death takes them or Allah ordains for them a way﴾. He did not clarify here whether He had ordained for them a way or not. However, He clarified in other places that He ordained for them the way by the prescribed punishment (hadd), as in His saying about the virgin: ﴿The fornicatress and the fornicator, flog each one of them…﴾ [al-Nur: 2], and His saying about the married person: "The old man and the old woman, if they commit adultery, stone them outright as a punishment from Allah, and Allah is Mighty and Wise." This is because this verse's ruling remains in force, as was authentically reported from the Commander of the Faithful, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him and make him content, even though its recitation has been abrogated.

It is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that the ruling on stoning is also derived from another verse that is muhkam (not abrogated in its recitation), namely His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, being called to the Book of Allah to judge between them, and then a faction of them turn away while they are refusing?﴾ For it was revealed concerning the Jewish man and Jewish woman who committed adultery while they were married, and the Prophet ﷺ stoned them. So His censure, in this Book, of those who turned away from what is in the Torah concerning the stoning of the married adulterer is clear Qur'anic evidence for the continuation of the ruling of stoning. What we have mentioned, that He, may He be exalted, ordained for them the way by the prescribed punishment, is further clarified by his saying ﷺ in the authentic report: "Take from me, Allah has ordained for them a way," (the hadith).

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those of your women who commit lewdness, bring against them four witnesses from among you; and if they testify, then confine them to the houses﴾, and so on.

(p-246) This verse indicates that the adulteress is not flogged but is confined until death or until Allah ordains for her a way.

Another verse has come that indicates she is not confined but is flogged one hundred lashes if she is a virgin, and a verse whose recitation is abrogated but whose ruling remains in force has come that she is stoned if she is married.

The answer is evident: the confinement of adulteresses in houses has been abrogated by flogging and stoning, or it had an end-point toward which it proceeds, which is Allah's ordaining a way for them; so Allah ordained the way by the prescribed punishment, as indicated by his saying ﷺ: "Take from me, Allah has ordained for them a way," (the hadith).

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not marry those women whom your fathers married﴾, to the end of the verse. In this noble verse Allah, may He be exalted, forbids marrying the woman whom the father has married. He did not specify what is meant by the father's marriage (p-230): is it the contract (al-'aqd) or the consummation (al-wat')? However, He clarified in another place that the term nikah (marriage) applies to the contract alone, even if no intercourse (masis) has taken place. This is in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49]. Thus He explicitly called it a nikah, and stated that there is no masis in it.

The scholars have agreed (ijma', i.e., scholarly consensus) that whoever the father has contracted marriage with becomes forbidden to his son, even if the father did not have intercourse with her. Likewise, the son's contract is forbidden to the father by consensus, even if he did not have intercourse with her. Allah, may He be exalted, has used the term nikah in another verse to mean intercourse after the contract. This is in His saying: ﴿And if he divorces her, she is not lawful to him thereafter until she marries another husband﴾ [al-Baqarah: 230]. The meaning of nikah here is not merely the contract; rather, intercourse must accompany it, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said to the wife of Rifa'ah al-Qurazi: "No, until you taste his honey and he tastes yours," meaning intercourse. There is no weight to what is narrated in opposition to this from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, because the clear and authentic text is decisive on this very question.

From here some scholars said: the word nikah is homonymous (mushtarak) between the contract and intercourse. Some said: it is literal (haqiqah) in intercourse and metaphorical (majaz) in the contract, because the contract is its cause. And some said the reverse.

Caution (tanbih)

Some scholars said: the particle ma in His saying ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married﴾ [al-Nisa': 22] is a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah). According to this, His saying "from the women" (min al-nisa') is connected to His saying "do not marry" and not to "married." The meaning on this view is: "Do not marry from among the women the marriage of your fathers," that is, do not do what your fathers used to do of corrupt marriage (nikah fasid). This view is the choice of Ibn Jarir. What appears, and what several verifying scholars affirmed decisively, is that ma is a relative pronoun (mawsulah) referring to the women whom the fathers married, as in His saying: ﴿So marry what is good for you of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 3]. We have already mentioned the reason for this, because they used to marry the wives of their fathers, as the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) indicates. Ibn Kathir narrated from Abu Hatim that its occasion of revelation was that "when Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat died, his son proposed to his wife. She asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about that, and he said: 'Return to your house.' So this verse was revealed: ﴿And do not marry what your fathers married﴾, to the end of the verse."

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: Marrying the wives of fathers was well known among the Arabs. Among those who did so was Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat mentioned above, for he married Umm Ubayd Allah, who had been under the marriage of his father al-Aslat. Al-Aswad ibn Khalaf married the daughter of Abu Talhah ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza ibn 'Uthman ibn 'Abd al-Dar, who had been under the marriage of his father Khalaf. Safwan ibn Umayyah married Fakhitah, the daughter of al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib ibn Asad, who had been under the marriage of his father Umayyah, as Ibn Jarir narrated from Ikrimah, saying that this was the occasion of revelation of the verse. 'Amr ibn Umayyah married his father's wife after him; she bore him Musafir and Abu Mu'ayt, and she had from Umayyah Abu al-'Is and others. So they were brothers of Musafir and Abu Mu'ayt and their paternal uncles. Mansur ibn Zabban ibn Sayyar al-Fazari married his father's wife Mulaykah bint Kharijah, as al-Qurtubi and others narrated. This Mulaykah is the one about whom Mansur, after 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) annulled his marriage to her, said:

[Al-Tawil]

Surely I do not care today what time may do, when Mulaykah is withheld from me, and wine.

If her visits have become far away, then greet the daughter of al-Murri at the rising of dawn.

The author of the poem 'Amud al-Nasab (the Pillar of Lineage) alluded to Mansur's marrying his father's wife in his saying, in mentioning the notable men of Fazarah:

[Al-Rajaz]

Mansur, the one who married in hatred, and swore fifty oaths that he had nothing, having stood on refusal.

As for his saying "and swore," etc.: its commentator said that its meaning is that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab made him swear fifty oaths after the 'Asr prayer in the mosque that the abrogation (naskh) of what the people of the Jahiliyyah practised, of marrying the wives of fathers, had not reached him. Al-Suhayli and others mentioned that Kinanah ibn Khuzaymah married the wife of his father Khuzaymah, and she bore him al-Nadr ibn Kinanah. He said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was born from marriage, not from illicit union," which indicates that this was permissible for them.

Ibn Kathir said: "There is scrutiny in what al-Suhayli narrated of the story of Kinanah." The author of 'Amud al-Nasab pointed to the weakening of what al-Suhayli mentioned in his saying:

[Al-Rajaz]

Hind bint Murr, mother of Harithah, is shakhish, and the mother of 'Anz is the third.

Barrah, their sister, was married to Khalaf, Kinanah, Khuzaymah, and Dif'.

Their sister 'Atikah, and her offspring: 'Udhrah, whom passion kills.

Its commentator said that the one who weakened this is al-Suhayli himself, contrary to the apparent statement of Ibn Kathir. The meaning of the verses is that Hind bint Murr, sister of Tamim ibn Murr ibn Udd ibn Tabikhah ibn Ilyas, is the mother of three of the sons of Wa'il ibn Qasit, namely al-Harith, Shakhish, and 'Anz; that their sister Barrah bint Murr was the wife of Khuzaymah ibn Mudrikah, and he married her after his son Kinanah; and that this is weak. And their sister 'Atikah bint Murr is the mother of 'Udhrah, the ancestor of the well-known tribe said to be killed by passion. Among the fabricated customs (mukhtalaqat) of the Arabs in the Jahiliyyah was the inheritance by relatives of the wives of their relatives. A man among them, when he died and his son or brother, for example, cast a garment over his wife, inherited her and became more entitled to her than she was to herself. If he wished, he married her without a dowry; if he wished, he married her to someone else and took her dowry; and if he wished, he withheld her (adal) until she ransomed herself from him. This continued until Allah forbade them from that, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, it is not lawful for you to inherit women by compulsion﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Nisa': 19]. The author of 'Amud al-Nasab alluded to this in his saying:

[Al-Rajaz]

The statement regarding what they differed about and invented, which only the hasty would be driven to.

Then he began enumerating their fabricated customs, until he said:

[Al-Rajaz]

And that whoever casts over his father's wife or the like, after she has become a widow, a garment showing it,

is more entitled to her than her own self: if he wishes, he marries her, or marries her off, or does evil,

by withholding her so that he inherits her, or so that she ransoms herself, and her dowry is for the two marriages to perdition.

The most apparent of the opinions regarding His saying: ﴿except what has already occurred﴾ [al-Nisa': 23] is that the exception is disjunctive (istithna' munqati'), meaning: but what has passed of committing this act before the prohibition is pardoned, as has been previously stated. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 23 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the wives of your sons who are from your loins﴾, etc. From it is understood that the wife of one's adopted son (da'i, the one he has adopted) is not forbidden to him. This understanding is expressed by Allah, may He be exalted, in His saying: ﴿So when Zayd had dissolved his marriage with her, We gave her to you in marriage, so that there would be no restriction upon the believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons when they have dissolved their marriages with them. And the command of Allah is ever accomplished﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37];
• and His saying: ﴿And He has not made your adopted sons your sons. That is your saying by your mouths﴾ [al-Ahzab: 4];
• and His saying: ﴿Muhammad is not the father of any one of your men﴾ [al-Ahzab: 40], etc.

As for the prohibition of the wife of a son through nursing (rida'), it is derived from an external proof, namely his (ﷺ) statement: "What is forbidden by blood kinship is forbidden by nursing," and Allah knows best.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):
His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that you join two sisters together﴾, etc.

This verse, by its generality, indicates the prohibition of combining any two sisters, whether they are joined by a contract or by right of possession (milk al-yamin). And there has come a verse which, by its generality, indicates the permissibility of combining two sisters by right of possession, namely His saying, may He be exalted, in Surat "Qad aflaha" and Surat "Sa'ala sa'il": ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess—for then they are not blameworthy﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 5–6].

So His saying ﴿And that you join two sisters together﴾ is a noun in the dual, defined by the article "al" (al-muhalla bi-al), and that which is defined by "al" is among the forms of generality, as is established and derived in the science of Usul (legal theory). And His saying ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ is a relative noun (ism mawsul), and it too is among the forms of generality, as is established in the science of Usul as well.

Between these two verses there is a partial generality and specificity (umum wa khusus min wajh) which causes them to conflict, as appears in the case of combining two sisters by right of possession. The generality of ﴿And that you join two sisters together﴾ indicates prohibition, while the generality of ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ indicates permissibility, as 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "One verse made them lawful, and another made them unlawful."

The summary of the resolution of the answer concerning these two verses is that the generality of one of them must be specified by the generality of the other. Thus preference (tarjih) between the two generalities becomes necessary, and the stronger of them is given precedence and the generality of the other is specified by it, because acting upon the stronger is obligatory by consensus. Accordingly, the generality of ﴿And that you join two sisters together﴾ is stronger than the generality of ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ for five reasons:

The first: The generality of ﴿And that you join two sisters together﴾ is explicit in the place of the intended ruling in itself, because the surah is Surat "an-Nisa'," in which Allah explained whom it is permitted to marry and whom it is forbidden. The verse ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ was not mentioned for the purpose of forbidding or permitting women; rather Allah mentioned the attributes of the God-fearing, and among them He mentioned guarding the private parts, and so it digressed to state that it is not required to guard it against the wife and the concubine. It is established in the principles that taking rulings from their proper sources is preferable to taking them from other than their proper sources.

The second: The verse ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ does not remain on its generality by the consensus of the Muslims, because a sister through nursing is not lawful by right of possession, by consensus, since the generality of ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ is specified by the generality of ﴿And your sisters through nursing﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]; and the woman a father has had intercourse with is not lawful by right of possession, by consensus, since the generality of ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ is specified by ﴿And do not marry what your fathers have married of women﴾ [al-Nisa': 22], etc.

The most correct view among the usulis regarding the conflict of a general term that has been subjected to specification with a general term that has not been subjected to specification is to give precedence to the one that has not been specified, and its reasoning is evident.

The third: The generality of ﴿And that you join two sisters together﴾ does not occur in the context of praise or blame, whereas the generality of ﴿or what their right hands possess﴾ occurs in the context of praising the God-fearing.

Scholars have differed regarding whether a general term occurring in the context of praise or blame retains its generality. Most scholars hold that its generality is valid, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be in bliss﴾ ﴿And indeed, the wicked will be in the Fire﴾ [al-Infitar: 13–14], for it encompasses every righteous person even though it is in the context of praise, and every wicked person even though it is in the context of blame.

Some scholars differed in this, including Imam al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, saying: a general term occurring in the context of praise or blame has no generality, because what is intended by it is encouragement in praise and deterrence in blame.

For this reason Imam al-Shafi'i did not take the generality of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 34] as applying to permissible ornaments, because the verse was given in the context of blame, so in his view it does not encompass permissible ornaments. When you have verified this, know that a general term not accompanied by something that prevents the consideration of its generality is preferable to one accompanied by something that, according to some scholars, prevents the consideration of its generality.

The fourth: Even if we concede the conflict between the two verses, the default regarding private parts is prohibition, until a proof that has no opposing evidence establishes permissibility.

The fifth: The generality that requires prohibition is preferable to that which requires permissibility, because leaving what is permissible is less severe than committing what is forbidden, as its verification will come, Allah willing, in Surat "al-Ma'idah," and Allah knows best.

These five aspects that we have explained are used to refute the argument of Dawud al-Zahiri from this noble verse for permitting the combining of two sisters in intercourse by right of possession. However, he argues from another verse, namely His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except what your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]. He says: the exception also refers back to His saying ﴿And that you join two sisters together﴾, so the meaning becomes: "And that you join two sisters together, except what your right hands possess," and in that case joining two sisters is not forbidden.

The return of an exception to all that precedes it of conjoined items, whether they are sentences or single words, is the practice according to the principles of Malik, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad, and to it points the statement of the author of Maraqi al-Su'ud [in rajaz meter]:
"Every case in which the conjunction precedes the exception, all of it stops, absent a proof from reason or revelation."

Contrary to Abu Hanifa, who holds that the exception returns only to the final sentence. Therefore he does not accept the testimony of a slanderer even if he repents and reforms, because His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except those who repent﴾ [al-Nur: 5], according to him, returns only to His saying: ﴿And it is they who are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Nur: 4], i.e., "except those who repent," since their defiance has ended by repentance; and he does not hold that it returns to His saying "and do not accept their testimony ever, except those who repent, then accept their testimony"; rather he says: do not accept their testimony in any case, since the exception in his view is restricted to the last clause.

Abu Hanifa did not contradict his principle in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except one who repents, believes, and does righteous work﴾ [al-Furqan: 70], where the exception returns to all the sentences before it, namely His saying: ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another deity, and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, and do not commit unlawful sexual intercourse﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], because all these sentences share their meaning with the final sentence, which is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever does that will meet a penalty﴾ [al-Furqan: 68], since the demonstrative in His saying "that" includes each of polytheism, killing and fornication; so by its return to the last clause it returned to all of them. Thus it is clear that Abu Hanifa did not contradict his principle in this case.

(p-249) And on account of this established principle in the science of Usul: if a man says, "This house is an endowment (habs) for the poor, the needy, the Banu Zuhrah and the Banu Tamim, except its wicked ones among them," then the wicked of all the groups are excluded according to the Malikis, Shafi'is and Hanbalis, contrary to the Hanafis, who say only the wicked of the last group are excluded.

On this basis, Dawud al-Zahiri's argument from this last verse is consistent with the principles of the Malikis, Shafi'is and Hanbalis.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: The verified position in this issue is what some later scholars verified, such as Ibn al-Hajib from the Malikis, al-Ghazali from the Shafi'is and al-Amidi from the Hanbalis, that the ruling concerning an exception that comes after a series of conjoined items is suspension (waqf), and that it is not to be judged as returning to all of them nor to the last one only. We say this is the verified position because Allah, may He be exalted, says: ﴿And if you disagree over anything, refer it back to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Nisa': 59].

When we refer this dispute back to Allah, we find that the Qur'an indicates the view of these scholars, which we have mentioned as the verified position, in many verses. Among them is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So the freeing of a believing slave and a compensation (diyah) delivered to his family, unless they give it as charity﴾ [al-Nisa': 92]. The exception returns to the diyah, so it falls away by the charity of its rightful recipient, and it does not return to the freeing of the slave, by unanimous agreement, because the recipient's charity of the diyah does not remove the expiation for accidental killing. Among them also is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So lash them eighty lashes and do not accept their testimony ever, and it is they who are the defiantly disobedient﴾ ﴿except those who repent﴾ [al-Nur: 4–5].

The exception does not return to His saying "lash them eighty lashes," because a slanderer's repentance does not remove the penalty for slander.

Among them also is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and do not take from among them a protector or a helper﴾ ﴿except those who reach a people between you and whom there is a treaty﴾ [al-Nisa': 89–90]. The exception in His saying ﴿except those who reach a people between you and whom there is a treaty﴾ does not return, by unanimous agreement, to the last clause, which is closest to it, namely His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and do not take from among them a protector or a helper﴾, since it is not permissible to take a protector or helper from among the disbelievers, even if they reach a people between you and whom there is a treaty. Rather, the exception returns to the seizing and killing in His saying: ﴿then seize them and kill them﴾, and the meaning is: seize them as captives and kill them, except those who reach a people between you and whom there is a treaty; so it is not permissible for you to seize them as captives nor to kill them, because the covenant held by those whom they reach prevents their capture and killing, as Hilal ibn 'Uwaymir al-Aslami stipulated in his peace agreement with the Prophet (ﷺ), since this verse was revealed concerning him, and concerning Suraqah ibn Malik al-Mudlaji, and concerning the Banu Judhaymah ibn 'Amir.

And if the exception sometimes does not return to the nearest clause to it in the Glorious Qur'an, which is at the highest level of inimitability, it becomes clear that it is not explicit in returning to other than it.

Among them also is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And were it not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan, except a few﴾ [al-Nisa': 83].

The exception does not return to the clause that immediately follows it, namely: ﴿And were it not for the favor of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have followed Satan﴾, because were it not for Allah's favor upon you and His mercy, you would all have followed Satan, and not a single one, few or many, would have been spared from that, so as to be excepted by the exception.

The scholars differed regarding the referent of this exception. It was said it returns to His saying: ﴿they spread it abroad﴾ [al-Nisa': 83]. It was said it returns to His saying: ﴿those among them who would know it by inference﴾ [al-Nisa': 83]. And if it does not return to the clause that follows it, then it is not explicit in its return to other than it. It was said that this exception returns to the clause that follows it, so it is not explicit in its return to other than it. It was said that this exception returns to the clause that follows it.

Accordingly, the meaning is: ﴿And had it not been for the grace of Allah upon you and His mercy﴾ by the sending of Muhammad, ﴿you would have followed Satan﴾ in the religion of your fathers, of disbelief and the worship of idols, ﴿except a few.﴾ Like those who were upon the religion of Ibrahim, such as Waraqah ibn Nawfal, Zayd ibn Nufayl, Qss ibn Sa'idah, and their likes.

Ibn Kathir mentioned that Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿you would have followed Satan, except a few﴾ that its meaning is: you would have followed Satan entirely. He said: The Arabs use "few" (qillah) while meaning "none" (adam). The proponent of this view cited the verse of al-Tirimmah ibn Hakim praising Yazid ibn al-Muhallab [Metre: al-Mutaqarib]:

"Noble, generous, frequenting many gatherings, few in blameworthy faults and reproaches."

He means: there is no blemish in him and no reproach.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: The use of "few" to mean "none" is very common in the speech of the Arabs, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"She kneeled down and cast a land upon a land, few therein are the voices except her bellowing."

He means that there is no sound in that desert other than the bellowing of his mount. And the saying of another:

"What harm would there be if she returned a greeting to us, a few [words], in the presence of one who knows the truth, finding fault with it?"

He means: there is no fault in it in the presence of one who knows the truth. On these last two views, there is no evidence in the verse. By this verification that we have established, the use of this last verse as evidence by Dawud al-Zahiri is also refuted, and knowledge is with Allah, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 24 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And [forbidden to you are] the married women, except those whom your right hands possess﴾. Know first that the word al-muhsanat (the chaste/married women) is used in the Qur'an in three senses:

(p-233) The first: al-muhsanat meaning the chaste women, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿chaste, not fornicators﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], i.e., chaste women who are not adulteresses.

The second: al-muhsanat meaning free women, as in His saying: ﴿Upon them is half the punishment of the chaste (muhsanat)﴾, i.e., upon slave women is half the lashing that is upon free women.

The third: that by ihsan is meant marriage (al-tazawwuj). This is definitively in His saying: ﴿And when they are married (uhsinna), if they commit indecency…﴾ the verse, i.e., when they marry. As for the statement of some scholars that the meaning of ihsan in His saying ﴿when they are married (uhsinna)﴾ is Islam, this goes against the apparent context of the verse, because the context of the verse concerns believing young women, where He says: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford [to marry] free believing women﴾ the verse.

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir of this verse, the exact wording being: "The most apparent, and God knows best, is that ihsan here means marriage, for the context of the verse indicates it, where He, glorified and exalted, says: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford [to marry] free believing women, then [he may marry] from what your right hands possess of your believing young women﴾ — and God knows best. The noble verse's context concerns believing young women, so it is determined that the meaning of His saying ﴿when they are married (uhsinna)﴾ is that they married, as Ibn 'Abbas and others explained." End of quotation; the point of relevance is in his words.

Having known this, know that in His saying, ﴿And the married women from among the women﴾ the verse, there are several interpretations, which are the opinions of scholars, and the Qur'an indicates the preference of one specific among them.

Some scholars said: the meaning of al-muhsanat here is more general than the chaste, the free and the married, i.e., all women are forbidden to you except those whom your right hands possess by a valid contract or by lawful ownership through slavery. The meaning of the verse on this view is the prohibition of all women except by a valid marriage or lawful concubinage. To this view went Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ata', and al-Suddi, and it is related from some of the Companions, and Malik chose it in al-Muwatta'.

Some scholars said: the meaning of al-muhsanat in the verse is free women, and on this view the meaning is: "And forbidden to you are free women other than the four, and lawful to you are what your right hands possess of slave women." On this view the exception is disjunctive (munqati').

Some scholars said: the meaning of al-muhsanat is the married women, and on this view the meaning of the verse is: "And forbidden to you are married women, because a woman with a husband is not lawful to another except what her right hands possess through captivity from the disbelievers, for captivity removes the earlier marital bond in disbelief." This view is the correct one, and it is the one the Qur'an indicates is correct. The first view entails applying "what the right hands possess" to include the ownership of marriage, whereas "ownership of the right hand" in the Qur'an has only come in the sense of ownership through slavery,

• as in His saying: ﴿then [marry] from what your right hands possess of your believing young women﴾,

• and His saying: ﴿and what your right hand possesses of what God has given you as spoils﴾ [al-Ahzab: 50],

• and His saying: ﴿and the companion at the side, and the wayfarer, and what your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nisa': 36],

• and His saying: ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 5, 6], in both places, making the ownership of the right hand a category distinct from marriage. And His saying: ﴿And those who seek a writing [of manumission] from among what your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nur: 33].

These verses indicate that what your right hands possess means slave women and not wives, as is apparent. Likewise the second view is not apparent, because its meaning would be: "And forbidden to you are free women, except what your right hands possess," and this contradicts the apparent meaning of the verse's wording, as you see.

Ibn al-Qayyim explicitly stated that this view is rejected both in wording and in meaning. It thus becomes clear that the context of the verse indicates the meaning we have chosen, just as the other verses we mentioned indicate it. It is also supported by the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), for its occasion of revelation, as Muslim recorded in his Sahih, and Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, and 'Abd al-Razzaq (narrated) from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may God be pleased with him, who said: "We captured captives from the captives of Awtas, and they had husbands, so we disliked having intercourse with them while they had husbands. So we asked the Prophet (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed: ﴿And the married women from among the women, except those whom your right hands possess﴾ [al-Nisa': 24], so we considered their private parts lawful [to us]."

Al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that it was revealed concerning the captives of Khaybar. A parallel to this correct interpretation is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

[Al-Tawil]
"And a woman with a husband whom our spears made wed (to us) is lawful to the one who consummates with her, she is not divorced."

* *

Caution (tanbih)

If it is said: the generality of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿except those whom your right hands possess﴾ is not restricted to captives. Rather, the apparent generality is that every married slave woman, when another man owns her, becomes lawful to him by ownership of the right hand, and the marital bond is removed by that ownership. And although the verse was revealed concerning captives specifically, as we mentioned, (p-235) the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the occasion. The answer: a group of the early scholars (salaf) held by the apparent generality, and ruled that the sale of a slave woman, for example, is a divorce for her from her husband, taking the generality of this verse. This view is reported from Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Hasan and Ma'mar, as Ibn Kathir and others transmitted from them. However, the verified position on this question is what we mentioned: that this ruling is restricted to captives and not to other owned persons acquired by another cause than captivity, such as sale for example, and this is not the specification of a general term by the occasion of its cause. The clearest proof of this is the well-known story of Barirah with her husband Mughith.

Ibn Kathir said in his tafsir of this verse, after mentioning the views of the group we mentioned that sale is a divorce: "The majority, early and recent, opposed them, and held that the sale of a slave woman is not a divorce for her, because the buyer is a deputy of the seller, and the seller had removed this usufruct from his ownership and sold her deprived of it. They relied in this on the hadith of Barirah recorded in the two Sahihs and elsewhere: 'Aisha, the Mother of the Believers, bought her and freed her, and her marriage to her husband Mughith was not annulled, rather the Messenger of God (ﷺ) gave her the choice between annulment and continuation, and she chose annulment.' Her story is well known. Had the sale of a slave woman been her divorce as these people say, the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have given her the choice; when he gave her the choice, this showed the marriage remained, and that the verse means only captives. And God knows best." End of quotation in his own words.

If it is said: if the buyer is a woman, the marriage is not annulled, because she does not own the enjoyment of a slave woman's womb, unlike a man, and ownership of the right hand is stronger than marital ownership, as a group said. The hadith of Barirah does not refute this view. The answer is what Ibn al-Qayyim articulated: if she does not own the enjoyment of her slave woman's womb, she owns the exchange over it and marrying her off and taking her dowry, and that is like the ownership of a man even if she does not enjoy the womb. When you have verified this, you know that the verified meaning of the verse, "And forbidden to you are the muhsanat," i.e., the married women, except what your right hands possess through captivity from the disbelievers, is that there is no prohibition in having intercourse with them by ownership of the right hand after istibra' (waiting period), because the earlier marital bond is dissolved by captivity, as we established. Umm al-Mu'minin Juwayriyah bint al-Harith, may God be pleased with her, had been married to a man named Musafi', and she was taken captive in the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq, and her story is well known. The author of Qurrat al-Absar said concerning Juwayriyah, may God be pleased with her:

[Al-Rajaz]
"He captured her in the raid of al-Mustaliq, from her husband Musafi', by al-Munzalaq."

By al-Munzalaq he means the sword. Then the scholars differed concerning captivity: does it nullify the earlier marital bond absolutely, even if the husband was captured with her, which is the apparent meaning of the verse, or does it not nullify it except when she alone is captured without him? If he was captured with her, the marital bond remains. This is the view of Abu Hanifa and some companions of Ahmad, and God knows best.

* *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So for what you have enjoyed from them, give them their wages﴾ the verse, meaning: just as you enjoy the women in marriage, give them their dowries in return for that. This meaning is supported by verses from the Book of God,

• such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And how would you take it when you have gone in unto one another﴾ the verse [al-Nisa': 21]. The "going in unto one another," which is explicitly stated as the cause for the full entitlement to the dowry, is the very same enjoyment mentioned here in His saying: ﴿So for what you have enjoyed from them﴾ the verse [al-Nisa': 24],

• and His saying: ﴿And give the women their dowries as a gift﴾ [al-Nisa': 4],

• and His saying: ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take back anything of what you have given them﴾ the verse [al-Baqarah: 229]. The verse concerns the marriage contract, not temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'ah), as said by one who does not know its meaning. If it is said: the expression "wages" (ujur) indicates that the intended meaning is the rent in temporary marriage, since the dowry is not called a wage, the answer is that the Qur'an called the dowry a wage in a place where there is no dispute: since the dowry, in return for enjoyment of the wife, as He explicitly stated in His saying: ﴿And how would you take it﴾ the verse, acquired a strong resemblance to the prices of benefits, it was called a wage. That place is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So marry them with the permission of their people and give them their wages﴾ the verse [al-Nisa': 25], i.e., their dowries, without dispute. Similar is His saying: ﴿And the chaste women from among the believing women and the chaste women from among those given the Book before you, when you have given them their wages﴾ the verse [al-Ma'idah: 5]. I.e., their dowries. Thus it is clear that the verse concerns marriage, not temporary marriage.

If it is said: Ibn 'Abbas, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and al-Suddi used to recite: "So for what you have enjoyed from them, until a specified term," and this indicates that the verse concerns temporary marriage, the answer is in three respects:

The first: their phrase "until a specified term" was not established as Qur'an, by the consensus of the Companions on its not being written in the 'Uthmanic codices. Most of the jurists of legal theory (usuliyyun) hold that what a Companion recited as Qur'an, but whose being Qur'an was not established, cannot be used as evidence for anything, because it is void from its origin: since he transmitted it only as Qur'an, and its being Qur'an is refuted, its invalidity becomes apparent from its origin.

The second: even if we proceed on the basis that it may be argued with, like the argument from solitary reports (khabar al-ahad), as some held, or on the basis that it is their exegesis of the verse in that sense, it is countered by something stronger, because the majority of scholars hold otherwise; and because the clear and sound hadiths are conclusive in great number on the prohibition of temporary marriage, and the Prophet (ﷺ) stated that this prohibition is permanent until the Day of Resurrection, as established in Sahih Muslim from the hadith of Sabrah ibn Ma'bad al-Juhani, may God be pleased with him, that he fought alongside the Messenger of God (ﷺ) on the day of the conquest of Makkah. He said: "O people, I had permitted you to enjoy women, and God has now forbidden that until the Day of Resurrection. Whoever has any of them, let him release her, and do not take back anything of what you have given them."

In a narration of Muslim concerning the Farewell Pilgrimage: there is no contradiction in this, since it is possible that he (ﷺ) said that on the day of the conquest of Makkah, and also at the Farewell Pilgrimage, and reconciliation (jam') is obligatory when possible, as is established in the science of legal theory and the sciences of hadith.

The third point: even if we grant, for the sake of argument, that the verse indicates the permissibility of mut'ah (temporary marriage), its permissibility has been abrogated (naskh), as the abrogation is established in the agreed-upon hadiths from him (ﷺ). It was abrogated twice: first on the day of Khaybar, as is established in the Sahih, and then on the day of the Conquest of Mecca, as is also established in the Sahih.

Some scholars said: it was abrogated only once, on the day of the Conquest. What occurred at Khaybar was the prohibition of the flesh of domestic donkeys only, and some narrators mistakenly thought that the day of Khaybar was also an occasion for the prohibition of mut'ah.

Ibn al-Qayyim chose this opinion. However, some authentic narrations explicitly state that mut'ah was also prohibited on the day of Khaybar. Therefore, the apparent view is that it was prohibited twice, as one or more scholars affirmed definitively, and this report is authentically transmitted. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

The fourth point: He, the Exalted, explicitly stated that it is obligatory to guard one's private parts from anyone other than a wife or a slave-woman, in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿except from their wives or those their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 6], in both places. Then He explicitly stated that whoever seeks beyond that is among the transgressors, in His saying: ﴿Then whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are the transgressors﴾, the verse [al-Mu'minun: 7].

It is known that the one who enjoys a mut'ah woman is neither a slave-woman nor a wife. Therefore, whoever seeks her is among the transgressors by the explicit text of the Qur'an. As for her not being a slave-woman, it is clear. As for her not being a wife, it is because the necessary consequences of marriage are absent from her, such as inheritance, the waiting period ('iddah), divorce, and maintenance. Had she been a wife, she would have inherited, observed the waiting period, been subject to divorce, and been owed maintenance, as is evident. Thus, this verse, which is: ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or those their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy; but whoever seeks beyond that, those are the transgressors﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 5–7, 29, 31], is explicit in prohibiting the enjoyment of women which has been abrogated. The context of the verse we are dealing with clearly indicates that the verse concerns the contract of marriage, as we have explained, not mut'ah marriage. This is because He, the Exalted, mentioned the forbidden women whom it is not permissible to marry in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers and your daughters﴾ [al-Nisa': 23], etc.

Then He clarified that other than those forbidden women are lawful through marriage, in His saying: ﴿And lawful for you is what is beyond that, that you seek them with your wealth, as chaste ones, not as fornicators﴾ [al-Nisa': 24]. Then He clarified that whoever you marry from among them and enjoy, it is obligatory for you to give them their dowry, linking this to the marriage with the particle "fa" (therefore) in His saying: ﴿So for whatever you have enjoyed from them, give them their compensation﴾, the verse [al-Nisa': 24], as we have clearly explained. And knowledge is with Allah the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford the means to marry free believing women, let him marry from those whom your right hands possess, from your believing young women﴾. The apparent meaning of this noble verse is that marrying a slave woman is not permissible, even in necessity, unless she is a believer, based on His saying: ﴿from your believing young women﴾ [an-Nisa': 25]. Its implication (mafhum al-mukhalafah, the implication of contrast) is that non-believing female slaves may not be married under any circumstances. This implication is also understood from another verse, His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the chaste women among those who were given the Scripture﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5], where "chaste women" is taken, according to one of the opinions, to mean free women. From it is understood that non-believing female slaves are not lawful to marry, even if they are People of the Book. Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, differed, so he permitted marrying a non-believing female slave, and permitted marrying female slaves to one who has the means to marry free women, because the implication of contrast is not considered valid in his principles, as is known in his legal theory, may Allah have mercy on him.

As for having intercourse with a non-believing female slave by right of ownership (milk al-yamin), if she is a People of the Book, then the majority of scholars hold that intercourse with her by ownership is permissible, based on the general sense of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except from their wives or what their right hands possess﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 6], and because marrying their free women is permissible, so concubinage with their female slaves is lawful. If the female slave owned by him is a Magian (majusiyyah) or a worshipper of idols, from among those whose free women are not lawful to marry, then the majority of scholars hold that intercourse with her by right of ownership is prohibited.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: "The jurists of the regions and the majority of scholars hold this view, and whatever opposes it is an aberration (shudhudh) that is not counted as a valid difference of opinion. The permissibility of this has not reached us except from Tawus."

The author, may Allah pardon him, said: "What appears from the standpoint of the evidence, and Allah knows best, is the permissibility of intercourse with a slave woman by right of ownership, even if she is a worshipper of idols or a Magian. This is because the majority of captives in his time, peace and blessings be upon him, were from the pagan Arabs, who were idol-worshippers, and it is not transmitted from the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, that he prohibited intercourse with them by ownership because of their disbelief. Had it been prohibited, he would have made it clear. Rather, he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: «A pregnant woman is not to be had intercourse with until she gives birth, nor a non-pregnant one until she menstruates once». He did not say 'until they embrace Islam'. Had that been a condition, he would have said it. The Companions took the captives of Persia, and they were Magians, and it is not transmitted that they abstained from them until they embraced Islam."

Ibn al-Qayyim said in Zad al-Ma'ad, his exact words: "This prophetic judgment indicates the permissibility of intercourse with idolatrous slave women by right of ownership. The captives of Awtas were not People of the Book. The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, did not make their embracing Islam a condition for intercourse with them, and did not make the only impediment anything other than the period of waiting (istibra'). Delaying the explanation beyond the time of need is impermissible, especially since they were recent converts to Islam, and the ruling of this matter would have been hidden from them, and all the captives (who were several thousands) embraced Islam, such that not a single slave girl among them remained aloof from Islam, which is known to be extremely unlikely. They were not compelled to embrace Islam, and they did not have such insight, desire and love for Islam as would necessitate all of them hastening to it. Therefore, the requirement of the Sunnah and the practice of the Companions during the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, and after him, is the permissibility of intercourse with owned women of whatever religion they were. This is the position of Tawus and others, and the author of al-Mughni strengthened it and preferred its evidences. And success is with Allah." End of Ibn al-Qayyim's words, verbatim, and it is very clear.

* * *

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when they are married, if they commit immorality, then upon them is half the punishment for free married women﴾. The punishment upon the free married women is not specified here, and this half falls upon the slave women. But it is specified in another place that it is one hundred lashes, by His saying: ﴿The adulterer and the adulteress, lash each one of them with one hundred lashes﴾ [an-Nur: 2]. From this it is known that the adulterous slave woman receives fifty lashes, and the adulterous male slave is likewise assimilated and receives fifty. The generality of "the adulteress" is specified by the text of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿then upon them is half the punishment﴾ [an-Nisa': 25], and the generality of "the adulterer" is specified by analogy (qiyas) to what is explicitly stated, because there is absolutely no difference between the free woman and the slave except slavery. Thus it is known that slavery is the cause of halving the lashes, and it is applied to the male slave because he shares the attribute of slavery, which is the basis (manat) of halving the lashes. This verse is, according to the usulis (jurists of legal theory), among the examples of specifying the generality of a text by analogy, based on the premise that the type of refining the basis known as eliminating the distinguishing factor (ilgha' al-fariq) is called analogy, and the dispute over whether it is analogy is well known in the principles. As for stoning, it is known that it is not halved, so it does not enter into the intended meaning of the verse.

Note

You have already learned from what preceded that the verified meaning of uhsinna is that it means "they married", and that is (p-240) its meaning on both readings, the reading with the verb in the active and in the passive. This differs from what Ibn Jarir chose, that the meaning of the reading ahsanna with a fatha on the hamza and sad, in the active, is "they embraced Islam", and that the meaning of uhsinna with a damma on the hamza and kasra on the sad, in the passive, is "they were married". On this basis, the implication of the condition in His saying: ﴿So when they are married﴾ [an-Nisa': 25] is that a slave woman who has not married has no hadd (prescribed punishment) upon her if she commits fornication, since He, may He be exalted, made her punishment in the verse dependent on her ihsan (being married). Ibn 'Abbas, Tawus, 'Ata', Ibn Jurayj, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu 'Ubayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam, and Dawud ibn 'Ali in one narration relied on the implication of this verse and said: there is no hadd upon a slave woman until she marries. The answer to this, and Allah knows best, is that the implication of this verse contains generality (ijmal), and the authentic Sunnah has clarified it. Its clarification is that linking the fifty lashes mentioned in the verse to the marriage of the slave woman implies that the slave woman who is not married is not thus only; it is possible that she is not lashed, and it is possible that she is lashed more than that or less, or stoned, or other possibilities. But the authentic Sunnah indicates that the unmarried slave woman is likewise, with no difference between her and the married one. The wisdom in mentioning specifically the married one is to avert the misconception that she is stoned like the free woman. Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) recorded in their two Sahihs from Abu Hurayrah and Zayd ibn Khalid al-Juhani, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they said: "The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked about a slave woman who commits fornication and is not married, and he said: 'If she commits fornication, lash her; then if she commits fornication, lash her; then if she commits fornication, lash her; then sell her, even for a rope (dafir)'."

Ibn Shihab said: "I do not know whether it was after the third or the fourth." Interpreting the lashing in the hadith as discipline (ta'dib) is not apparent, especially since in some narrations the hadd is explicitly stated. So the implication of this verse is precisely what the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was asked about, and in this agreed-upon hadith he answered by ordering lashing. The apparent reason the questioner asked was that the implication of this verse was unclear to him. The hadith is therefore a clear text on the point in dispute. Had the lashing of the unmarried slave woman been more or less than that of the married one, he, peace and blessings be upon him, would have explained it.

By this you know that the opinions contrary to this are not to be relied upon, such as the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and those who agreed with him, mentioned just above, and the saying that the unmarried slave woman is lashed one hundred times, which is what is known from Dawud ibn 'Ali al-Zahiri, and its remoteness is not hidden; and like the saying that the married slave woman is stoned and the unmarried is lashed fifty, which is the view of Abu Thawr, and the extreme remoteness of this is not hidden. And knowledge is with Allah, may He be exalted.
