As for Imam Abu Hanifa (may God have mercy on him), the one he prefers among them is that the imam prays with the first group one rak'ah if he is travelling, or if it is, for example, the dawn prayer, and two rak'ahs if he is resident. Then this first group goes to face the enemy, then the other group comes and he prays with them what remains of the prayer and gives the salam. This last group goes to face the enemy, and the first group comes and completes the rest of its prayer without recitation, because they are lagging behind (lahiq). Then they go to face the enemy, and the other group comes and completes the rest of its prayer with recitation, because they are those who were overtaken (masbuq). They based this manner on the hadith of Ibn 'Umar mentioned above. We have already mentioned that this manner is not in the narration of the two Sahihs and elsewhere for the hadith of Ibn 'Umar.

We have also mentioned earlier, from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud in Abu Dawud, that when the other group had prayed with the Prophet (ﷺ) the other rak'ah (p-260), they completed for themselves, so they joined the two rak'ahs together, then went to face the enemy, and the first group came and prayed their remaining rak'ah. This is the summary of the four schools' positions on the prayer of fear.

Al-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: The prayer of Dhat al-Riqa' is more excellent than the prayer of Batn Nakhl according to the more correct of the two opinions, because it is more balanced between the two groups, and because it is validly established by consensus, whereas that one (Batn Nakhl) is the prayer of one obligated behind one performing a supererogatory prayer, and on it there is disagreement among the scholars. The second opinion, which is the view of Abu Ishaq, is that the prayer of Batn Nakhl is more excellent, because each group attains the merit of a complete congregation. Know that in a resident (hadari) situation the imam prays with each of the two groups two rak'ahs, and in a travelling (safari) situation one rak'ah each. In the maghrib prayer he prays with the first group two rak'ahs according to the majority.

Some have said: he prays with the first group in maghrib one rak'ah. Know that the verified view is that the expedition of Dhat al-Riqa' took place after Khaybar, even though a large number of historians firmly held that the expedition of Dhat al-Riqa' was before Khaybar. The evidence for this is the authentic hadith that the arrival of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari to the Prophet (ﷺ) was when he conquered Khaybar, together with the authentic hadith that Abu Musa witnessed the expedition of Dhat al-Riqa'.

al-Bukhari said in his Sahih: Muhammad ibn al-'Ala' narrated to me, Abu Usama narrated to us, Buraid ibn 'Abdullah narrated to us, from Abu Burda, from Abu Musa (may God be pleased with him), who said: "The news of the Prophet's (ﷺ) emigration reached us while we were in Yemen, so we set out as emigrants to him, I and two of my brothers, I being the youngest of them: one of them was Abu Burda and the other Abu Ruhm, - he said either 'in some number' or 'fifty-three' or 'fifty-two men' of my people. We boarded a ship, and our ship carried us to the Negus in Abyssinia. We met Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and stayed with him until we all came, and we met the Prophet (ﷺ) when he had conquered Khaybar." The hadith... In it there is an explicit statement that Abu Musa's arrival was at the conquest of Khaybar.

Al-Bukhari also said: Muhammad ibn al-'Ala' narrated to us, Abu Usama narrated to us, from Buraid ibn Abi Burda, from Abu Burda, from Abu Musa (may God be pleased with him), who said: "We went out with the Prophet (ﷺ) on an expedition, and we were six men, among us one camel which we rode in turns, and our feet became torn, my feet became torn and my nails fell out, and we used to wrap rags around our feet. Therefore it was named the expedition of Dhat al-Riqa'." The hadith... These two authentic hadiths contain clear evidence that Dhat al-Riqa' was after Khaybar. Al-Bukhari (may God have mercy on him) said: "Chapter: The expedition of Dhat al-Riqa', which is the expedition against the warriors of Khasafa from Banu Tha'laba of Ghatafan, so he camped at Nakhl; and it was after Khaybar, because Abu Musa came after Khaybar, etc." We have only clarified this so that it may be known that there is no proof, from the non-performance of the prayer of fear in the expedition of the Trench, that it is legislated in a resident situation, on the claim that Dhat al-Riqa' was before the Trench and that the prayer of fear was legislated before the Battle of the Confederates, which is the Battle of the Trench; and that he (ﷺ) did not abandon it even though they had occupied him and his Companions from the Zuhr and 'Asr prayers until night. Rather, the verified view is that the prayer of fear was not legislated until after the Trench. Ahmad al-Badawi al-Shinqiti, in his poetic composition on the battles, alluded to the expedition of Dhat al-Riqa' with these words:

Then against Muharib and Tha'laba, at Dhat al-Riqa', they struck the enemy hard.
There was no war between them and Ghawrath, as happened with Da'thawr.
With the Prophet, and according to the reliable view, it occurred once, without multiplicity.

The compiler of this poem holds that it was revealed before Khaybar, following Ibn Sayyid al-Nas and those who agreed with him. Among the points on which the scholars differed regarding the forms of the prayer of fear (ṣalāt al-khawf) is the prayer of Dhī Qarad. In it, each group prays one rak'ah with the Imam and confines itself to that. We have already cited this from the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas in Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, al-Nasāʾī and Ibn Mājah, and from the hadith of Ḥudhayfah in Abū Dāwūd and al-Nasāʾī. This is the form that Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamān performed when Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ said at Ṭabaristān: "Which of you prayed the prayer of fear with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?" Ḥudhayfah said: "I did," and he led them in the manner we have mentioned, as al-Nasāʾī narrated from him, and from Zayd ibn Thābit. Abū Dāwūd related it from Thaʿlabah ibn Zahdam, and al-Nasāʾī related it through the same chain. The wording of Abū Dāwūd from Thaʿlabah ibn Zahdam is: "We were with Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ at Ṭabaristān, when he stood up and said: 'Which of you prayed the prayer of fear with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ?' Ḥudhayfah said: 'I did.' So he led these people in one rak'ah and those in one rak'ah, and they did not make up the rest."

Abū Dāwūd said: Likewise it was narrated by ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah and Mujāhid, from Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Prophet ﷺ; by ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaqīq, from Abū Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ; by Yazīd al-Faqīr; and by Abū Mūsā.

Abū Dāwūd said: "A man from the Successors, not al-Ashʿarī, all of them from Jābir, from the Prophet ﷺ." Some narrators have said, from Shuʿbah, regarding the hadith of Yazīd al-Faqīr, that they made up one more rak'ah. Likewise Simāk al-Ḥanafī narrated it from Ibn ʿUmar, from the Prophet ﷺ, and likewise Zayd ibn Thābit narrated from the Prophet ﷺ: "So the people had one rak'ah each, and the Prophet ﷺ had two rak'ahs." End of his quotation, in his own words.

Al-Qurṭubī said in his *Tafsīr*, and his text is: "al-Suddī said: If you pray two rak'ahs while travelling, it is complete, and shortening is not permitted except when you fear. This verse permits each group to pray one rak'ah without adding anything to it, while the Imam has two rak'ahs. Something similar was narrated from Ibn ʿUmar, Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allah and Kaʿb, and Ḥudhayfah did it at Ṭabaristān when the commander Saʿīd ibn al-ʿĀṣ asked him about it. It was also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that the Prophet ﷺ prayed in this way at the battle of Dhī Qarad, one rak'ah for each group, and they did not make it up. It was narrated from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allah that the Prophet ﷺ prayed in this way with his companions on the day of the battle of Muḥārib Khaṣfah and Banī Thaʿlabah. Abū Hurayrah related that the Prophet ﷺ prayed in this way between Ḍajnān and ʿUsfān." And according to this, each of the two groups confines itself to one rak'ah.

Ishāq also said: It was narrated from Imam Aḥmad and the majority of scholars that confining oneself to one rak'ah in fear is not permitted. They answered the hadiths reporting this in two ways.

The first: that what the Companions who related it meant by "and they did not make it up" is that, after they were safe and the fear had passed, they did not make up that prayer which they had prayed in a state of fear. The benefit of this is that one who was afraid, once safe, does not repeat what he prayed in that form, which differs from the form of prayer in safety. This view has some basis in reasoning.

The second: that their statement in the hadith, "and they did not make it up," means according to the knowledge of the one who related it, because another narrator has related that they did make up one rak'ah in that same prayer. The version of the one who adds is preferred. This was said by al-Qurṭubī and Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr. What supports it is what preceded from the narration of Yazīd al-Faqīr from Jābir through the route of Shuʿbah in Abū Dāwūd, that they made up another rak'ah. The affirming report takes precedence over the negating one. This narration is further supported by the multitude of authentic reports that do not confine the prayer of fear to a single rak'ah in its forms. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

* *

The sum of the forms of the prayer of fear whose explanation has preceded is five: the prayer of close combat (*ṣalāt al-musāyafah*), which is established in the explicit text of the Qur'an; the prayer of Baṭn Nakhl; the prayer of ʿUsfān; the prayer of Dhāt al-Riqāʿ; and the prayer of Dhī Qarad. Shaykh Aḥmad al-Badawī al-Shinqīṭī, in his poem on the military expeditions, alluded to the expedition of Dhāt Qarad with his words, in rajaz metre:

Ghazwat al-Ghābah, which is Dhū Qarad, when he went out after his camels and found them.
Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ pursued them, while he was saying: "Today is the day of the suckling ones."
The Guide assigned him two shares, for his outrunning the horses on foot,
And they rescued from the son of Ḥiṣn ten [captives], and the Prophet divided among them camels.

Al-Bukhārī, in his *Ṣaḥīḥ*, affirmed that the expedition of Dhāt Qarad took place three nights before Khaybar. Muslim in his *Ṣaḥīḥ* related something similar from Iyās ibn Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ, from his father, who said: "We returned from the expedition to Madinah. By Allah, we did not stay in Madinah except three nights before we set out for Khaybar." Therefore nothing in the authentic report is more reliable than what the people of the biographies (*ahl al-siyar*) mention in contradiction to it, such as the statement of Ibn Saʿd that it was in Rabīʿ al-Awwal of the sixth year before Ḥudaybiyyah, and the statement of Ibn Isḥāq that it was in Shaʿbān of the sixth year, a few days after the expedition of Laḥyān.

Ibn Ḥajar in *Fatḥ al-Bārī* inclined to reconcile what is in the authentic hadith with what the people of the biographies mention, by the repetition of the going out to Dhī Qarad. Qarad is with two fatḥahs in the narration of the hadith, while the lexicographers mention that it is with a ḍammah then a fatḥah, or with two ḍammahs. The prayer of fear has been reported in other forms besides those we have mentioned.

Ibn al-Qaṣṣār the Mālikī said: The Prophet ﷺ prayed it in ten places.

Ibn al-ʿArabī the Mālikī said: It was narrated "from the Prophet ﷺ that he prayed the prayer of fear twenty-four times."

The one who restricts it (its author), may Allah pardon him, says: What appears to be correct, and Allah the Exalted knows best, is that the best of the forms established from him ﷺ in the prayer of fear is the one that is most thorough in caution for the prayer and in safeguarding against the enemy.

* *

Two remarks

The first: this verse of the prayer of fear is among the clearest proofs for the obligation of congregational prayer, because the command to perform it in this difficult situation is clear evidence that it is a binding command. For if it were not binding, it would not have been commanded in a time of fear, since fear is an evident excuse.

The second: the prayer of fear is not restricted to the Prophet ﷺ. Rather its legislation remains until the Day of Resurrection. The argument for its being specific to him ﷺ, based on the Exalted's words ﴿And when you are among them and lead them in prayer﴾ (Q 4:102), is a baseless argument. The Companions and all Muslims have unanimously rejected the like of it in the words ﴿Take from their wealth a charity to purify them﴾ (Q 9:103). The condition that he be among them was stated only to explain the ruling, not to make it a requirement of its existence. The meaning is: explain to them by your action, since action is clearer than speech, as Ibn al-ʿArabī and others said. Abū Yūsuf, al-Muzanī, al-Ḥasan ibn Ziyād, al-Lu'lu'ī and Ibrāhīm ibn ʿUlayyah departed from the majority and said the same as them. They said: The prayer of fear was not legislated after him ﷺ, and they argued from the implicature of the condition (*mafhūm al-sharṭ*, the understanding of the contrary by a condition) in His words ﴿And when you are among them﴾. This was answered by the consensus of the Companions upon it after him ﷺ, and by his ﷺ words: "Pray as you have seen me praying." The general wording of this hadith takes precedence over that implicature.

* *

A remark

You have established the preference that the verse ﴿And when you travel in the land, there is no blame upon you for shortening the prayer﴾ (Q 4:101) refers to the prayer of fear and not to the prayer of travel. Then the implicature of the condition in ﴿And when you travel in the land﴾ would imply that the prayer of fear is not legislated in residence.

The answer: this implicature was held by Ibn al-Mājishūn, who prohibited the prayer of fear in residence. Some also argued for prohibiting it there by saying that the Prophet ﷺ did not pray it on the day of the Trench, and he missed the two afternoon prayers and made them up after sunset, and that he ﷺ prayed it only while travelling. The majority of scholars hold that it is also prayed in residence. They answered that the condition has no contrary implicature (*mafhūm mukhālafah*) either, because it follows what is usual, as has preceded, or because it was revealed concerning a specific event, explaining its ruling.

As narrated from Mujāhid, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ and his companions were at ʿUsfān, and the polytheists were at Ḍajnān. They met, and the Prophet ﷺ prayed with his companions a complete prayer with its bowing and prostrations. The polytheists resolved to raid their goods and baggage," and then the verse was revealed. This event occurred while they were travelling, striking the earth. It has been established in the principles of jurisprudence that among the impediments to considering the implicature of contrariness (*mafhūm al-mukhālafah*) is that the statement was revealed concerning an actual event. For this reason the implicature of contrariness was not considered in His words ﴿if they desire chastity﴾ (Q 24:33), nor in His words ﴿Let not the believers take the disbelievers as allies instead of the believers﴾ (Q 3:28), because each of them was revealed concerning an actual event.

The first was revealed concerning the coercion by Ibn Ubayy of his slave-girls into fornication, when they wished to remain chaste. The second was revealed concerning a group of the Anṣār who befriended the Jews instead of the believers. The Qur'an came down in each case forbidding the situation that occurred, without intending to restrict the ruling to it. This was alluded to in *al-Marāqī*, in his enumeration of the impediments to considering the implicature of contrariness, with his words:

Or a favour, or the agreement with the reality, or ignorance, or emphasis in the hearer's mind.

(p-265) They answered regarding his ﷺ not praying it on the day of the Trench that this was before the prayer of fear was revealed, as al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Ḥibbān and al-Shāfiʿī related. From this you know that the statement of one who said that the battle of Dhāt al-Riqāʿ, in which the Prophet ﷺ prayed the prayer of fear, took place before the Trench is not correct. They answered regarding his not praying it except while travelling that travel, in relation to the prayer of fear, is a descriptive attribute (*waṣf ṭardī*, one that does not restrict), and its cause is fear, not travel. Whenever fear exists, its ruling exists, as is evident.

* *

A point

If it is said: why should each form of the prayer of fear not abrogate (*naskh*) the ones before it, since they used to act on the latest of them? The answer is in two parts:

The first is what has preceded, that the enemy is sometimes in the direction of the qiblah and sometimes not in its direction, and so on as has preceded. In each situation the form suitable to it is performed, as is evident.

The second is what some of the jurists investigated, such as Ibn al-Ḥājib, al-Rahūnī and others, that actions have no contradiction between them at all. For an action occurs in external reality only as a particular instance, not as a universal, so as to negate another action. The action that occurs has no common measure shared between it and another. So it is permissible for one action to be obligatory at one time and, at another time, the opposite. Accordingly there is no obstacle to the permissibility of two actions differing in form for one and the same act of worship. He set this down in *Marāqī al-Suʿūd* with his words:

And the conflict of actions has not been in every state of the states.

What al-Maḥallī mentioned, that action indicates continuing permissibility without speech, was examined by the author of *Nashr al-Buntūd* in his commentary on the verse just preceding. And knowledge is with Allah the Exalted.

* *

His Exalted words in this noble verse, ﴿lest those who disbelieve should attack you﴾ (Q 4:101), mean: they may harm you. Branch issues connected with this noble verse, on the view that it concerns shortening the four-rak'ah prayer, as is understood from the hadith of Yaʿlā ibn Umayyah from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with them both, from the Prophet ﷺ, in Muslim, Aḥmad and the authors of the Sunan, as has preceded:

First branch: The scholars have agreed on the legitimacy of shortening the four-rak'ah prayer while travelling, contrary to whoever deviated and said: there is no shortening except in Ḥajj or ʿUmrah; and whoever said: there is no shortening except in fear; and whoever said: there is no shortening except on a journey of obedience only. These are opinions on which the people of knowledge do not rely. The scholars differed over full prayer while travelling: is it permissible or not? Some scholars held that shortening while travelling is obligatory.

And among those who held this view was Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, and it is the view of ʿAlī, ʿUmar, and Ibn ʿUmar. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbās and Jābir, and al-Thawrī held it. Al-Khaṭṭābī, in *al-Maʿālim* (a commentary on Sunan Abī Dāwūd), attributed it to the majority of the early scholars (ʿulamāʾ al-salaf) and the jurists of the major cities (fuqahāʾ al-amṣār). He also attributed it to ʿAlī, ʿUmar, Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, Qatādah, and al-Ḥasan. He said: "Ḥammād ibn Abī Sulaymān said: whoever prays four rak'ahs while travelling must repeat the prayer." End of quotation, transmitted through al-Shawkānī, may Allah have mercy on him.

The evidence for this view, which is the obligation of shortening the prayer, is the hadiths we mentioned earlier from ʿĀʾishah, Ibn ʿAbbās, and ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them, that the prayer was originally made obligatory as two rak'ahs; then the travel prayer was left as it was, and the prayer of residence was increased. The evidence of these scholars is clear.

A group of scholars went to the permissibility of both completing and shortening the prayer, just as fasting and breaking the fast are both permissible. However, they differed over whether shortening or completing is better. ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, and ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with them, held this view.

al-Nawawī said in *Sharḥ al-Muhadhdhab*, and al-ʿAbdarī transmitted it from these people, meaning those we have mentioned, as well as from Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Mālik, Aḥmad, Abū Thawr, and Dāwūd. It is the position of the majority of scholars. al-Bayhaqī narrated it from Salmān al-Fārisī among twelve Companions, and from Anas, al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Aswad, Ibn al-Musayyab, and Abū Qilābah. The proponents of this view argued with several points:

The first: the words of Allah, Exalted, ﴿There is no blame upon you if you shorten the prayer﴾ [an-Nisāʾ: 101]. The expression "no blame" indicates that it is not obligatory.

The second: what we mentioned earlier in the hadith of Yaʿlā ibn Umayyah from ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, that "the Prophet ﷺ said concerning shortening the prayer while travelling: 'It is a charity which Allah has given to you as a gift'..." (the hadith continues). That it is a charity and a concession indicates that it is not obligatory.

The third: what al-Nasāʾī, al-Bayhaqī, and al-Dāraquṭnī narrated, "from ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she performed ʿumrah with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He broke his fast and shortened the prayer, while she fasted and completed the prayer. She informed him of that, and he said to her: 'You have done well.'"

al-Nawawī said in *Sharḥ al-Muhadhdhab*: this hadith was narrated by al-Nasāʾī, al-Dāraquṭnī, and al-Bayhaqī (p-267) with a fair or sound isnad (chain of transmission). He said: al-Bayhaqī said in *al-Sunan al-Kubrā*: al-Dāraquṭnī said its isnad is fair (ḥasan). He said in *Maʿrifat al-Sunan wa-al-Āthār*: it is a sound isnad.

The compiler of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: The apparent position is that what came in this hadith, that the ʿumrah of ʿĀʾishah mentioned was in Ramadan, is not authentic. This is because the established fact, based on sound reports, is that the Prophet ﷺ never performed ʿumrah in Ramadan at all, for he performed only four ʿumrahs:

The first: the ʿumrah of al-Ḥudaybiyah, in which the polytheists blocked him from the Sacred House, in the sixth year.

The second: the ʿumrah of the making-up (ʿumrat al-qaḍāʾ), which was the agreed term of the truce at al-Ḥudaybiyah, and it was in the seventh year.

The third: the ʿumrah from al-Jiʿrānah after the conquest of Makkah, in the eighth year. All these three ʿumrahs took place in the month of Dhū al-Qaʿdah, by consensus and by sound reports.

The fourth: his ʿumrah together with his Ḥajj during the Farewell Pilgrimage. The narration of al-Nasāʾī does not state that the ʿumrah mentioned was in Ramadan. Its wording is: "Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā al-Ṣūfī informed me, saying: Abū Nuʿaym narrated to us, saying: al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Zuhayr al-Azdī narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Aswad narrated to us, from ʿĀʾishah: that she performed ʿumrah with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from Madinah to Makkah. When she arrived in Makkah she said: 'O Messenger of Allah, may my father and mother be your ransom, you shortened and completed, you broke your fast and I fasted.' He said: 'You have done well, O ʿĀʾishah,' and he did not find fault with me." End of quotation.

The fifth: what is narrated from ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, "that the Prophet ﷺ used to shorten the prayer while travelling and also complete it, and break his fast and also fast."

al-Nawawī said in *Sharḥ al-Muhadhdhab*: it was narrated by al-Dāraquṭnī, al-Bayhaqī, and others.

al-Bayhaqī said: al-Dāraquṭnī said its isnad is sound. Ibn Ḥajar, in *al-Talkhīṣ*, recorded it with the wording "yaqṣuru" with a ya' (so the subject is the pronoun of the Prophet ﷺ), and "tutimmu" with two tāʾs (so its subject is a pronoun referring to ʿĀʾishah). This would have the same meaning as the first hadith. However, in some narrations of the hadith there is an explicit attribution of the completion to the Prophet ﷺ.

al-Bayhaqī said: Abū Bakr ibn al-Ḥārith, the jurist, informed us; ʿAlī ibn ʿUmar, the ḥāfiẓ, informed us; al-Maḥāmilī narrated to us; Saʿīd ibn Muḥammad ibn Thawāb narrated to us; Abū ʿĀṣim narrated to us; ʿUmar ibn Saʿīd narrated to us, and from (p-268) ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ, from ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "that the Prophet ﷺ used to shorten the prayer and also complete it, and break his fast and also fast." ʿAlī said: this is a sound isnad. End of quotation.

al-Bayhaqī said: it has a supporting report from the hadith of Dalham ibn Ṣāliḥ, al-Mughīrah ibn Ziyād, and Ṭalḥah ibn ʿAmr, and all of them are weak.

The fifth argument: the consensus of the scholars that a traveller who follows an resident imam in prayer must complete the prayer. Had shortening been an absolute obligation, it would not have been permissible to pray four rak'ahs behind the imam.

The proponents of this view answered the hadiths of ʿUmar, ʿĀʾishah, and Ibn ʿAbbās by saying that what is meant by the travel prayer being two rak'ahs is: for whoever wishes to do so. As for ʿUmar's words in the hadith, "complete, not shortened," they said its meaning is that it is complete in reward. This was said by al-Nawawī, but it is not free from strained interpretation.

The proponents of the first view answered the arguments of these people, saying: the words of Allah, Exalted, ﴿There is no blame upon you if you shorten the prayer﴾ [an-Nisāʾ: 101] refer to the prayer of fear (ṣalāt al-khawf), as we mentioned earlier, so there is no evidence in it for shortening the four-rak'ah prayer. They said: even if we accept that it refers to shortening the four-rak'ah prayer, the expression ﴿and there is no blame upon you﴾ [an-Nisāʾ: 102] does not contradict obligation, as you acknowledged with a parallel in the words of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Indeed, aṣ-Ṣafā and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah. So whoever makes ḥajj to the House or performs ʿumrah – there is no blame upon him for going back and forth between them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 158], because the sa'y (walking between aṣ-Ṣafā and al-Marwah) is obligatory according to the majority.

As for his words in the hadith, "a charity which Allah has given to you," they said that the Prophet ﷺ commanded accepting it in his words, "so accept His charity," and a command requires obligation. Therefore we do not have the option of not accepting it, given his words ﷺ, "so accept it."

As for the third and fourth points, they answered that the two hadiths of ʿĀʾishah mentioned are not authentic, neither of them. They supported the invalidity of these reports by what is established in the Ṣaḥīḥ from ʿUrwah that she interpreted her completion of the prayer in the same way that ʿUthmān interpreted it. Had she possessed a report from the Prophet ﷺ on this matter, ʿUrwah would not have said that she interpreted it.

Ibn al-Qayyim said in *Zād al-Maʿād*, and his words are as follows: "I heard Ibn Taymiyyah say: this hadith is a lie upon ʿĀʾishah. ʿĀʾishah would not have prayed contrary to the prayer of the Prophet ﷺ and the rest of the Companions, while she saw them shortening, and then she alone completed it without any reason. How could that be, when she is the one who said: 'The prayer was made obligatory as two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs, then the prayer of residence was increased, and the travel prayer was left as it was.' So how can it be supposed that she would add to what Allah prescribed and oppose the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his Companions?"

az-Zuhrī said to Hishām ibn ʿUrwah, when he narrated to him from his father, from her, about this matter: "Then what is the reason that she used to complete the prayer?" (p-269) He said: "She interpreted it as ʿUthmān interpreted it." Then he said: "If the Prophet ﷺ approved her act and confirmed it, then there is no basis for interpretation at that point, and it is not valid to attribute her completion to interpretation under this assumption. Ibn ʿUmar informed that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did not add to two rak'ahs while travelling, nor did Abū Bakr nor ʿUmar. Could it be supposed of ʿĀʾishah, the Mother of the Believers, that she opposed them while she saw them shortening? After his death ﷺ, she completed as ʿUthmān completed, and both interpreted. The proof lies in their narration, not in the interpretation of one of them when others disagree with him. And Allah knows best." End of quotation; the relevant point is quoted in its own words.

The compiler of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: As for finding it unlikely that ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, opposed the Prophet ﷺ during his lifetime while acknowledging that she opposed him after his death, this implies that opposing him after his death is permissible. There is no doubt that the prohibition of opposing him during his lifetime remains after his death ﷺ. It is therefore not lawful for anyone at all to oppose what he brought of guidance until the Day of Resurrection, whether in action, in word, or in tacit approval. It is not fully evident that ʿĀʾishah opposed the guidance of the Messenger ﷺ through ijtihād (independent reasoning). The report of the one who narrated that she interpreted implies the denial of her narration from the Prophet ﷺ about this matter, while the hadith mentioned affirms that she narrated it from him, and the affirming report takes precedence over the negating one. On this basis, this hadith is strengthened, the one that some scholars declared sound and some declared fair, as has been mentioned.

The verification is that the isnad of al-Nasāʾī mentioned earlier, through which he narrated this hadith, is sound. As for Ibn Ḥibbān's criticism of it on the ground that it includes al-ʿAlāʾ ibn Zuhayr al-Azdī, and that he said of him: "he narrates from trustworthy narrators what does not resemble the hadith of established reports, so reliance on him is invalid," this is rejected, because al-ʿAlāʾ mentioned is trustworthy (thiqah), as Ibn Ḥajar stated in *al-Taqrīb* and elsewhere. And the criticism of some scholars that ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Aswad did not meet ʿĀʾishah is rejected, because he did meet her.

al-Dāraquṭnī said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān met ʿĀʾishah; he entered upon her while he was a youth (murāhiq). al-Ṭaḥāwī mentioned from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān that he entered upon ʿĀʾishah after seeking permission following his reaching puberty. The author of *al-Kamāl* mentioned that he heard from her. al-Bukhārī in his *Tārīkh* and Ibn Abī Shaybah mentioned what supports this. Ibn Ḥajar said this. The criticism of the hadith mentioned, that it is irregular (muḍṭarib), because some narrators say "from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Aswad, from his father, from ʿĀʾishah," and some say "from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from ʿĀʾishah," is also rejected, because the narration of the one who said "from his father" is an error, and the correct version is "from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn al-Aswad, from ʿĀʾishah."

al-Bayhaqī said after citing the chains of both narrations: Abū Bakr al-Naysābūrī said: "Thus Abū Nuʿaym said, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from ʿĀʾishah, and whoever said 'from his father' in this hadith has erred." End of quotation.

Therefore, the apparent position is that this hadith is established, and it strengthens the argument of those who did not prohibit completing the four-rak'ah prayer while travelling, and they are the majority of scholars. Imam Mālik ibn Anas held that shortening the four-rak'ah prayer while travelling is a sunnah, and that whoever completes it must repeat it within its time. This is because it is established that the Prophet ﷺ was consistent in shortening during his journeys, and likewise Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿUthmān, except on the days of Minā. Mālik did not prohibit completing it, because of the evidences we mentioned. And Allah knows best.

* *

The second branch: The scholars differed over determining the distance at which the prayer is shortened. Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Aḥmad said: it is four barīds, and a barīd is four farsakh, and a farsakh is three miles, and approximately by time it is the distance of two days' travel at a moderate pace. Among them there is a known difference concerning the length of the mile. Those who held this view used as evidence what Mālik narrated from Ibn Shihāb, from Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh, from his father, that he rode to Rīm and shortened the prayer on that journey.

Mālik said: That is about four barīds, and Rīm is a place. One of the poets of Madinah said:

*"How many a lava field lies between al-Munaqqā and Uḥud, and the sides of Rīm."*

And by what Mālik narrated from Nāfiʿ, from Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh, that ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar rode to Dhāt al-Nuṣub and shortened the prayer on that journey.

Mālik said: Between Dhāt al-Nuṣub and Madinah is four barīds. And with what Mālik said: it reached him that ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAbbās used to shorten the prayer at a distance like that between Makkah and al-Ṭāʾif, and at a distance like that between Makkah and ʿUsfān, and at a distance like that between Makkah and Jeddah.

Malik said: That is four barids, and that is the most preferred (distance) to me for which prayer is shortened. And by what Malik narrated from Nafi' that he used to travel with Ibn 'Umar a barid and would not shorten the prayer. All these reports mentioned are in the "Muwatta'," and among those who said this were Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas, as we have mentioned from them.

Al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, said in his "Sahih": Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, used to shorten and break their fast over four barids, which is sixteen farsakh. End quote. Al-Hasan al-Basri, al-Zuhri, al-Layth ibn Sa'd, Ishaq and Abu Thawr also held this view, as al-Nawawi transmitted from them. A group of the people of knowledge held that shortening is not permitted for less than a journey of three days. Among those who said this was Abu Hanifah, and it is the opinion of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, Suwayd ibn Ghaflah, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan ibn Salih, and al-Thawri. Also from Abu Hanifah is (the view of) two days and most of a third. The proponents of this view argued with the hadith of Ibn 'Umar and the hadith of Abu Sa'id, both authentic in the Sahih: that the Prophet ﷺ said: "A woman should not travel three days except with a mahram accompanying her," and with the hadith: "The traveller's wiping over the khuff is for three days and their nights." The basis of the argument with this last hadith is that it implies that every traveller is prescribed wiping for three days, and generality in this is only valid if the minimum duration of travel is set at three days, for if it were set at less than that, he could not complete its duration, since his journey would have ended; therefore this requires that it be estimated at three, otherwise some travellers would be excluded from it. End quote.

The argument from the two hadiths is not apparent to me, as it seems: the meaning of the first hadith is that it is not lawful for a woman to travel a distance of three days except with a mahram, and this does not indicate defining the least that is called travel. What supports this is that it occurs in some authentic narrations: "A woman should not travel two days except with her husband or a mahram."

And in some authentic narrations: "It is not lawful for a woman who believes in Allah and the Last Day to travel a distance of a day and a night without a mahram with her." In a narration of Muslim it is "a distance of a day," and in another of his it is "a night," and in a narration of Abu Dawud: "Do not travel a barid." Al-Hakim also narrated it and said: its chain is sahih.

Al-Bayhaqi said in "al-Sunan al-Kubra": These narrations concerning three, two, and one day are all authentic, "and it seems that the Prophet ﷺ was asked about a woman travelling three (days) without a mahram, and he said: 'No.' He was asked about her travelling two days without a mahram, and he said: 'No.' And (about) one day, and he said: 'No.' Each one of them transmitted what he memorized, and none of these numbers is a limit for travel." End quote from him, in his wording.

It thus becomes clear that the derivation of the minimum travel from the hadith is not sound, as you see, especially since Ibn 'Umar, its narrator, opposed it as has passed, and the principle with the Hanafis is that what matters is what the Companion saw, not what he narrated.

As for the argument from the hadith fixing the wiping of the traveller at three days with their nights, it too is not sound, because if his journey ends before them he becomes a resident and the name of travel no longer applies to him. The hadith does not state that he must travel for three days; the most the hadith conveys is that the traveller has the period of three days for wiping over the khuff. If he remains a traveller for it, then that is so; if he completes his journey before it, he is no longer a traveller, and there is no difficulty in that.

A group of the people of knowledge held that shortening is permitted for a full day's journey; among those who said this were al-Awza'i and Ibn al-Mundhir. They argued with what has preceded in some authentic narrations, that the Prophet ﷺ applied the name of travel to a distance of one day, and travel is the basis (manat) of shortening. Also with what Malik narrated in the "Muwatta'" from Ibn Shihab, from Salim ibn 'Abd Allah, that 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar used to shorten the prayer over a full day's journey. The apparent practice of al-Bukhari is that he prefers that it is a day and a night, for he said: "Chapter: On how much one shortens the prayer, and the Prophet ﷺ named a day and a night as travel." The statement "and the Prophet ﷺ named..." etc., following his heading "On how much one shortens the prayer," indicates that this is, in his view, the basis of shortening, as is apparent.

Some scholars held that shortening is permitted for both short and long travel. Among those who said this was Dawud al-Zahiri, of whom some people of knowledge said: even if he went out to a garden outside the town, he would shorten. The proponents of this view argued with the unrestricted (wording of) the Book and Sunnah permitting shortening without restriction of distance, and with what Muslim narrated in his "Sahih" from Yahya ibn Yazid al-Hana'i, who said: I asked Anas ibn Malik about shortening the prayer, and he said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ, "when he went out a distance of three miles or three farsakh" (Shu'bah being in doubt), "prayed two rak'ahs." This is the wording of Muslim. And with what Muslim also narrated in the "Sahih" from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, who said: "I went out with Shurahbil ibn al-Simt to a village seventeen or eighteen miles away, and he prayed two rak'ahs. I said to him, so he said: I saw 'Umar pray two rak'ahs at Dhu al-Hulayfah, so I asked him, and he said: I only do as I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ do."

The majority answered that there is no evidence in the two hadiths of Muslim mentioned, because what is meant by them is not that the distance mentioned in them is the limit of travel; rather their meaning is that when he undertook a long journey and moved away three miles, he shortened. This is because it is apparent that he ﷺ did not travel when the time of prayer entered except after he had prayed it, so the next prayer would not reach him except after he had moved away from Madinah. Likewise is the hadith of Shurahbil mentioned. As for the statement that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, prayed two rak'ahs at Dhu al-Hulayfah, it is to be understood in line with what we have mentioned in the hadith of Anas, namely that he was travelling to Makkah or elsewhere, passed by Dhu al-Hulayfah, and the prayer reached him, so he prayed two rak'ahs; not that Dhu al-Hulayfah was the limit of his journey. This was said by al-Nawawi and others, and it has a basis in reasoning. Nothing explicitly transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ about shortening is reported for less than two stages (marhalatayn), as al-Nawawi affirmed.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: Ibn Hajar said in "Talkhis al-Habir": Sa'id ibn Mansur narrated from Abu Sa'id who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when he travelled one farsakh, would shorten the prayer, and he remained silent about it." If it is authentic, it is clearly evidence for shortening prayer over a short distance, with a clearer indication than the two hadiths of Muslim mentioned earlier.

The author, may Allah pardon him, says: This which we have mentioned is the essence of the scholars' statements on defining the distance of shortening, and it appears that there is no explicit text defining it, and it has been disputed upon in roughly twenty opinions. What al-Bayhaqi, al-Daraqutni and al-Tabarani narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "O people of Makkah, do not shorten (the prayer) for less than four barids," is weak, because its chain includes 'Abd al-Wahhab ibn Mujahid, who is abandoned (matruk), and al-Thawri called him a liar.

Al-Azdi said: Narrating from him is not lawful, and his narrator from him is Isma'il ibn 'Ayyash, and his narration from other than the Syrians is weak; and the 'Abd al-Wahhab mentioned is Hijazi, not Syrian. The correct position regarding this hadith is that it is mawquf upon Ibn 'Abbas, narrated from him by al-Shafi'i with a sahih chain, and Malik narrated it from him in the "Muwatta'" as a balagh, and we have already mentioned it.

It appears that the disagreement over defining the distance is of the type of disagreement over verifying the manat (the applicable cause): whatever is called travel in the Arabic language, shortening is permitted in it, because this is the apparent sense of the texts, and no valid transmission has diverted it. Mere leaving of the town is not called travel, and the Prophet ﷺ used to go to Quba' and to Uhud and did not shorten the prayer. The two hadiths we have mentioned from Muslim are open to interpretation, and the hadith of Sa'id ibn Mansur mentioned earlier: we do not know whether it is sahih or not. If it is sahih, it would be a strong text on shortening the prayer over both short and long distances. The shortening of the people of Makkah with the Prophet ﷺ during the Farewell Pilgrimage is, according to some scholars, evidence for shortening over a non-long distance, while some say the shortening is at Muzdalifah, Mina and 'Arafat, which are among the rites of Hajj. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

The author, may Allah pardon him, says: The strongest of the opinions in argument, as it appears to me, is the view of whoever said that everything called travel, even if short, is a context in which the prayer is shortened, because of the unrestricted use of "travel" in the texts, and because of the two hadiths of Muslim mentioned earlier, and the hadith of Sa'id ibn Mansur. Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated from Waki', from Mis'ar, from Muharib, who said: I heard Ibn 'Umar say: "Indeed, I travel at an hour of the day and I shorten (the prayer)."

Al-Thawri said: I heard Jabalah ibn Suhaym say: I heard Ibn 'Umar say: "If I went out a mile I would shorten the prayer."

Ibn Hajar said in "al-Fath": The chain of each of them is sahih. End quote. And knowledge is with Allah the Exalted.

* *

The third branch: The traveller begins shortening when he passes the houses of his town, meaning he has left the entire town. He does not shorten in his house once he intends travel, nor in the middle of the town. This is the view of the majority of scholars, including the four Imams and most of the jurists of the major cities. It is established from the Prophet ﷺ that he shortened at Dhu al-Hulayfah. Malik's position is that if the town has inhabited orchards, their ruling is that of the town, so one does not shorten until one passes them. The majority argued that one shortens only upon leaving the town, because shortening is conditional on "striking the earth" (al-darb fi al-ard), and whoever has not left the town has not struck the earth. Some scholars held that if he intends travel he shortens while still in his dwelling. Ibn al-Mundhir mentioned from al-Harith ibn Abi Rabi'ah that he intended a journey, and so he prayed two rak'ahs with them in his dwelling, and among them was al-Aswad ibn Yazid, and more than one of the companions of Ibn Mas'ud. He said: We have also related its meaning from 'Ata' and Sulayman ibn Musa. He said: Mujahid said: The traveller does not shorten during the day until night enters, and if he sets out at night he does not shorten until day enters. From 'Ata': when he passes the walls of his house, he has the right to shorten.

Al-Nawawi said: These two views are invalid. The view of Mujahid contradicts the authentic hadiths about the Prophet ﷺ shortening at Dhu al-Hulayfah when he left Madinah, and the view of 'Ata' and those who agree with him contradicts the concept of travel. End quote from him, and it is apparent, as you see.

* *

The fourth branch: The scholars differed over the length of the stay which, if the traveller intends to remain for it, obliges him to complete the prayer. Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, and Ahmad in one of his two narrations held that it is four days. The Shafi'is say: the day of entry and the day of departure are not counted. Malik says: if he intends to stay four full days, he completes.

Ibn al-Qasim said, concerning al-'Utaybah: the day of his entry is disregarded and not counted. The well-known narration from Ahmad is that it is more than twenty-one prayers.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 101 (part 7 of 7):

Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is half a month. Those who hold that it is four days argue with what is established in the Sahih from the hadith of al-'Ala' ibn al-Hadrami, may Allah be pleased with him, that he heard the Prophet ﷺ say: "The muhajir may remain in Makkah for three nights after the completion of his rites (al-sadr)." This is the wording of Muslim. In another narration from him via Muslim: "The muhajir has the allowance of staying three nights in Makkah after al-sadr." And in another narration from him: "The muhajir remains in Makkah three days after completing his rites (nusuk)." Al-Bukhari also related it in the Manaqib, from al-'Ala' ibn al-Hadrami as well, with the wording: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Three (nights) for the muhajir after al-sadr." End of quote. They say: the Prophet ﷺ permitted the muhajirun to stay three days, which indicates that whoever stays for them is in the ruling of the traveller, and that whatever exceeds them is residence (iqamah), and the one who resides must complete the prayer. Also with what Malik related in al-Muwatta' with a sound chain, from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he expelled the Jews from the Hijaz, then permitted those among them who came as merchants to stay three days.

This evidence has been answered from the side of the opponent: the Prophet ﷺ only granted them leave for three nights because that is the period in which their needs are typically met and their affairs prepared for travel. Likewise 'Umar's permission to the Jews to stay three days. The argument mentioned for the view of four days has a basis in reasoning, because it is supported by analogy: shortening (qasr) was prescribed to lighten the hardship of travel, and whoever stays four days, that is the period in which the hardship of travel is removed from him.

Imam Ahmad argued that the number [of prayers shortened] is not more than twenty-one prayers, with what is established in the Sahih from the hadith of Jabir and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the Prophet ﷺ "arrived in Makkah during the Farewell Pilgrimage at dawn on the fourth day, and the Prophet ﷺ stayed the fourth, fifth, sixth and seventh days, and prayed the Fajr at al-Abtah on the eighth day. He was shortening the prayer during these days, and he had resolved to stay for them, and they are twenty-one prayers, because they are four full days plus the Subh prayer of the eighth." He said: so when one resolves to stay as the Prophet ﷺ stayed, he shortens; and when he resolves to stay longer than that, he completes.

Al-Athram related from Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, that this argument is speech that not everyone understands. Imam Ahmad interpreted the hadith of Anas, "that the Prophet ﷺ stayed in Makkah during the Farewell Pilgrimage for ten (days), shortening the prayer," according to this meaning that we mentioned from him, and that Anas intended the duration of his stay in Makkah, Mina and Muzdalifah.

The one who restricts it (muqayyiduhu), may Allah pardon him, says: this should not be departed from, due to the clarity of its reasoning and the evident fact that it is the truth.

Note
The hadith of Anas, which is established in the Sahih, is not contradicted by what is also established in the Sahih from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ stayed in Makkah nineteen (days), shortening the prayer." So when we travel and stay nineteen (days), we shorten; and if we stay longer, we complete. This is because the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas concerns the conquest (ghazwat al-Fath), while the hadith of Anas concerns the Farewell Pilgrimage, and the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas is to be understood as meaning that the Prophet ﷺ was not intending to reside; and mere residence without intention does not break the ruling of travel according to the majority, and Allah knows best.

Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, argued that it is half a month, with what Abu Dawud related through Ibn Ishaq, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stayed in Makkah in the year of the Conquest for fifteen (days), shortening the prayer." An-Nawawi, in al-Khulasah, weakened the narration of fifteen.

Al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar said in al-Fath: "This is not good, because its narrators are trustworthy, and Ibn Ishaq is not alone, for al-Nasa'i related it through 'Iraq ibn Malik, from 'Ubayd Allah, from Ibn 'Abbas in the same way." Abu Hanifah chose the narration of fifteen over the narrations of seventeen, eighteen and nineteen, because it is the least that has been reported, so the others are interpreted as having occurred by coincidence; but the most preponderant and most frequently transmitted of the narrations in the sound reports is the narration of nineteen, and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh adopted it. Al-Bayhaqi reconciled the narrations: whoever said nineteen counted the day of entry and the day of departure; whoever said seventeen omitted both; and whoever said eighteen omitted one of them.

As for the narration of fifteen, the apparent explanation is that the narrator thought the original was seventeen and deducted from it the day of entry and the day of departure, so the remainder became fifteen.

Know that there are several opinions of the scholars concerning residence without intention:
One: that he completes after four days.
Second: after seventeen days.
Third: eighteen.
Fourth: nineteen.
Fifth: twenty days.
Sixth: he shortens always until he resolves to reside.
Seventh: for the combatant (al-muharib) to shorten; and for others, shortening is not allowed after four days of residence.

The most apparent of these opinions is that one does not shorten until he intends to reside, even if his stay is prolonged without intention of residence. It is supported by the Prophet's ﷺ shortening during his stay in Makkah in the year of the Conquest, as established in the Sahih; and by what Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Hibban and al-Bayhaqi related from Jabir, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ stayed in Tabuk twenty days, shortening the prayer." This hadith was declared sound by an-Nawawi and Ibn Hazm, but al-Daraqutni, in al-'Ilal, gave it a defect of irsal and inqita' (interruption in the chain), and that 'Ali ibn al-Mubarak and others among the memorizers related it from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Thawban as a mursal report; and that al-Awza'i related it from Yahya from Anas, and said: "bidh'a 'ashrah" (a few ten [days]); and with this wording al-Bayhaqi related it, and it is weak.

Al-Bayhaqi said after relating it: "I do not consider it preserved; and it has been related from another route from Jabir with: 'bidh'a 'ashrah'." End of quote. The narration of al-Awza'i on this point has been disputed; al-Daraqutni mentioned it in al-'Ilal and said: "The sound report from al-Awza'i from Yahya is that Anas used to do it." Ibn Hajar said: "Yahya did not hear from Anas."

An-Nawawi said in Sharh al-Muhadhdhab: "I say: the narration of the musnad was related solely by Ma'mar ibn Rashid, who is an imam whose eminence is agreed upon, and the rest of the chain is sound according to the conditions of al-Bukhari and Muslim; so the hadith is sound, because the correct position is that when a hadith contradicts between irsal and isnad, the musnad is given the ruling." End of quote from him. The author of al-Maraqi put this in verse:

"Raising (of a mursal to a musnad) and connection, and an addition in wording, are accepted by the imam of memorization..." etc.

He also argued, for the view that mere residence without intention does not break the ruling of travel, with what Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi related from the hadith of 'Imran ibn Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "I fought alongside the Prophet ﷺ and witnessed the Conquest with him, and he stayed in Makkah eighteen nights, praying only two rak'ahs, saying: 'O people of the town, pray four, for we are travellers.'" The Prophet's ﷺ saying in this hadith, "for we are travellers," together with his residence for eighteen (nights), clearly indicates that one who resides without intention of residence is still called a traveller. This is supported by the hadith: "Actions are only by intentions." This hadith was graded hasan by al-Tirmidhi, but its chain contains 'Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, who is weak.

Ibn Hajar said: al-Tirmidhi graded his hadith as hasan because of its corroborating reports, and did not consider the disagreement concerning the duration, as is known from the custom of the hadith scholars, who consider agreement on the chains but not the context. End of quote. 'Ali ibn Zayd mentioned above was related by Muslim in conjunction with others.

al-Tirmidhi said of his hadith on travel: hasan sahih; and said: "He is truthful, and perhaps raised what was stopped (mawquf)," and Ya'qub ibn Shaybah declared him trustworthy.

Some scholars said: he became confused in his old age; Shu'bah, al-Thawri, 'Abd al-Warith and many others related from him.

Al-Daraqutni said: "There is only some weakness in him." The apparent truth is that al-Daraqutni's statement is closer to the correct view concerning him, but what came after his confusion is to be avoided from him. End of quote. Besides this, there are other evidences that residence without intention does not break the ruling of travel. "The Companions stayed in Ramahurmuz for nine months, shortening the prayer." Al-Bayhaqi related it with a sound chain, and its weakening by 'Ikrimah ibn 'Ammar is rejected, since this 'Ikrimah is among the narrators of Muslim in his Sahih.

Ahmad in his Musnad related from Thumamah ibn Sharahil, from Ibn 'Umar, that he said: "I was in Adharbayjan, I do not know whether he said four months or two months, and I saw them praying two rak'ahs, two rak'ahs." Al-Bayhaqi also related it. Ibn Hajar said in al-Talkhis: its chain is sound. End of quote.

The position of Malik is to distinguish between an army in the land of war, where he does not shorten, and others, where he shortens with the intention of residing four full days.

[[The author's words have been abridged due to their great length]]

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 103 (part 1 of 7):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers as a decree of specified times﴾. In this noble verse He mentions that prayer was and still is a prescribed obligation upon the believers, meaning something written upon them as a binding and definite duty, "specified" (mawqut), meaning it has times that become obligatory upon their entry. He does not indicate those times here, but He indicates them in other places, such as His saying: ﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night, and [also] the recitation of dawn. Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾ [al-Isra: 78]. By His saying ﴿at the decline of the sun﴾, which is its passing from the middle of the sky, according to verification, He points to the Zuhr and 'Asr prayers; by His saying ﴿until the darkness of the night﴾, which is its darkness, He points to the Maghrib and 'Isha' prayers; and by His saying (p-280) ﴿and the recitation of dawn﴾ He points to the Subh prayer, and He expressed it as "recitation" in the sense of recitation, because recitation is a pillar within it, by way of expressing a thing by the name of one of its parts.

This explanation has been made fully clear by the Sunnah in a comprehensive manner. Among the verses in which the times of prayer are indicated, as several scholars have said, is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So glory be to Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning﴾ ﴿And to Him is praise in the heavens and the earth - and [glorify Him] at night and when you are at noon﴾ [al-Rum: 17, 18]. They said: the intended glorification in this verse is prayer. By His saying ﴿when you enter the evening﴾ He points to the Maghrib and 'Isha' prayers; by His saying ﴿and when you enter the morning﴾ He points to the Subh prayer; by His saying ﴿and at night﴾ He points to the 'Asr prayer; and by His saying ﴿and when you are at noon﴾ He points to the Zuhr prayer. And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day and at the approach of the night﴾ [Hud: 114]. The closest of the opinions regarding the verse is that by "the two ends of the day" He points to the Subh prayer at its beginning and the Zuhr and 'Asr prayers at its end, meaning in its latter half; and by "approach of the night" He points to the Maghrib and 'Isha' prayers.

Ibn Kathir said: It is possible that the verse was revealed before the obligation of the five prayers, and the obligatory prayers before it were two: a prayer before the rising of the sun, and a prayer before its setting, along with qiyam al-layl (night prayer). Then this was abrogated (naskh) by the five prayers. On this basis, the intended "two ends of the day" are the prayer before the rising of the sun and before its setting, and the intended "approach of the night" is qiyam al-layl.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: The apparent position is that this possibility mentioned by the memorizer Ibn Kathir, may Allah have mercy on him, is remote, because the verse was revealed concerning Abu al-Yasar in Madinah some time after the prayers were obligated; so it indicates, according to verification, the times of prayer. It is a Madinan verse within a Makkan surah. These are the details of the times of prayer, with their evidences from the Sunnah that explain them. It is not hidden that each of these times has a beginning and an end. As for the beginning of the time of Zuhr, it is the decline of the sun from the middle of the sky, by the Book, the Sunnah and the consensus. As for the Book, it is His saying: ﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun﴾; the lam here indicates timing, and "dulook al-shams" is its passing from the middle of the sky, according to verification.

As for the Sunnah, among it is the hadith of Abu Barzah al-Aslami in the two Sahihs: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to pray the al-Hajirah, which you call the first, when the sun declines (tadhhadu)..." and the hadith; and tadhhadu means it passes from the middle of the sky.

In a narration of Muslim: "when it passes (tazul)." In the two Sahihs, from Jabir (raDiyallahu 'anhu): "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to pray Zuhr at al-Hajirah." In the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Anas (raDiyallahu 'anhu) that he "went out when the sun had declined, and prayed Zuhr." In the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "Jibril led me in prayer at the door of the House twice; he prayed Zuhr with me when the sun had passed its zenith..." the hadith. It was narrated by the two Imams al-Shafi'i and Ahmad, Abu Dawud, Ibn Khuzaymah, al-Daraqutni, and al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak, and he said: a sahih hadith.

al-Tirmidhi said: a hasan hadith. If it is said that its chain includes 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn 'Ayyash ibn Abi Rabi'ah, and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi al-Zinad, and Hakim ibn Hakim ibn 'Abbad ibn Hunayf, and all of them are disputed, the answer is: they were followed in it, for 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated it from al-'Umari, from 'Umar ibn Nafi' ibn Jubayr ibn Mut'im, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, similarly.

Ibn Daqiq al-'Id said: it is a good supporting narration (mutaba'ah hasanah), and Ibn al-'Arabi and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr authenticated it, although in some of its narrations the chain does not include 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi al-Zinad but rather Sufyan, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith mentioned, from Hakim ibn Hakim mentioned; so this narration is free from weakness by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi al-Zinad. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr also narrated it by this route and said: the objection to its chain has no basis. Likewise Abu Dawud, Ibn Khuzaymah and al-Bayhaqi narrated it by this route.

And from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah (raDiyallahu 'anhuma) that "Jibril (peace be upon him) came to the Prophet and said to him: 'Rise and pray,' and he prayed Zuhr when the sun had declined..." the hadith. It was narrated by Imam Ahmad, al-Nasa'i, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim.

al-Tirmidhi said: Muhammad, meaning al-Bukhari, said: the hadith of Jabir is the most authentic thing on the times (al-mawaqit).

'Abd al-Haqq said: meaning concerning the leading of Jibril in prayer, and this is apparent.

And from Buraydah (raDiyallahu 'anhu) that "a man asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the time of prayer, and he said: 'Pray with us these two days.' When the sun declined, he commanded Bilal (raDiyallahu 'anhu), who gave the adhan, then he commanded him and he called the iqamah for Zuhr..." the hadith, narrated by Muslim in his Sahih. And from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (raDiyallahu 'anhu) that "a questioner came to the Prophet (ﷺ) asking him about the times of prayer, until he said: then he commanded him, and he established Zuhr when the sun had declined, and the speaker was saying: the day has reached its midpoint, and he was more knowledgeable than them" the hadith, also narrated by Muslim. The narrations on this topic are very numerous.

As for consensus, all Muslims have agreed that the beginning of the time of the Zuhr prayer is the declining of the sun from the middle of the sky, as is necessarily known from the religion of Islam.

* *

As for the end of the time of the Zuhr prayer, the apparent position from the evidences of the Sunnah concerning it is that it is when the shadow of every thing becomes equal to it, without considering the shadow of the zawal (noon shadow). For in the hadiths mentioned above, on the first day he prayed 'Asr when the shadow of every thing had become equal to it in the leading of Jibril, and that is at the end of the time of Zuhr. The most explicit of these is what Muslim narrated in his Sahih from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr (raDiyallahu 'anhuma), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The time of the Zuhr prayer is as long as the 'Asr has not arrived." This sahih hadith indicates that when the time of 'Asr comes, the time of Zuhr has gone. The well-known narration from Malik, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, is that what we have mentioned as its limit by the evidences is the preferred time (al-waqt al-ikhtiyari) of Zuhr, and that its necessary time (al-waqt al-darury) extends in common with 'Asr until the setting of the sun.

Similar to this has been narrated from 'Ata' and Tawus. The apparent position is that the proof of the people of this view is the evidences indicating that Zuhr and 'Asr share a time. From the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas mentioned earlier: "he prayed Zuhr on the second day at the time at which he had prayed 'Asr on the first." And also from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) combined (jama'a) at Madinah without fear or travel," agreed upon; and in a narration of Muslim: "without fear or rain." They took this as evidence for the sharing of time, and they also said: the prayers were increased upon the explanation of Jibril on the second day, so the time of Zuhr should be increased as well.

The author of these notes, may Allah pardon him, says: The apparent position is that this argument falls. As for the argument for sharing from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, "he prayed Zuhr on the second day at the time at which he had prayed 'Asr on the first day," the answer to it is what al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, answered: the meaning of his praying Zuhr on the second day is his finishing from it, as is the apparent sense of the wording; and the meaning of his praying 'Asr at that time on the first day is the beginning of the prayer. So he finished the Zuhr prayer on the second day when the shadow of the person equaled him, and began the 'Asr prayer on the first day when the shadow of the person equaled him as well. Thus sharing is not implied, and there is no difficulty in this, because the end of the time of Zuhr is the beginning of the time of 'Asr. What supports the correctness of what al-Shafi'i said is what Muslim narrated in his Sahih from the hadith of Abu Musa (raDiyallahu 'anhu): "and he prayed Zuhr close to the time of 'Asr the previous day." This is a sound and clear proof that he began the Zuhr prayer on the second day close to the time when the shadow of the person equals him, and completed it when his shadow equaled him, as is apparent. Similar to this interpretation that al-Shafi'i adopted is His saying: ﴿And when they have reached their term, then retain them﴾ [al-Talaq: 2], and His saying: (p-283) ﴿And when they have reached their term, do not prevent them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 232]. So the meaning of the first "reaching" is its approach, and the second is the actual completion of the term.

As for the argument for sharing from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, agreed upon, that he (ﷺ) "combined at Madinah without fear or travel," the answer is that it must be understood as a formal combining (al-jam' al-suwari), as a way of reconciling the evidences: that he prayed Zuhr at the end of its time, when only enough time remained in it for its performance, and upon finishing it the time of 'Asr entered, so he prayed it at its beginning. Whoever prays Zuhr at the end of its time and 'Asr at the beginning of its time, his prayer has the appearance of combining, while in reality there is no combining, because he performed each of the two prayers in its specified time, as is apparent. More explanation of this will come, if Allah wills.

As for the argument that the prayers were increased upon the explanation of Jibril, it is clearly invalid, because the timing of acts of worship is determined by revelation (tawqifi) without dispute, and the increase in the stated times was established by the legal texts.

* *

As for the 'Asr prayer, the texts of the Sunnah indicate that it has a preferred time and a necessary time. As for its preferred time, its beginning is when the shadow of every thing becomes equal to it, without considering the shadow of the zawal, and its time enters upon the ending of the time of Zuhr previously explained. In the previously mentioned hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: "he prayed 'Asr when the shadow of every thing had become equal to it."

In the previously mentioned hadith of Jabir as well: "he prayed 'Asr when the shadow of every thing had become equal to it," and this is the verified position concerning the beginning of the time of 'Asr, as the mentioned hadiths and others have stated explicitly.

al-Shafi'i said: the beginning of the time of 'Asr is when the shadow of every thing becomes equal to it, and it adds a slight addition.

[p-284] The author of these notes, may God pardon him, says: If al-Shafi'i meant that the addition (of a measure) is to establish clearly that the shadow has reached its equal, since that cannot be known with certainty without some addition, as some Shafi'is have said, then his view agrees with that held by the majority and does not oppose it. If he meant something other than this, then it is rejected by the explicit texts stating that the beginning of the time for 'Asr is when an object's shadow equals it, without any need for an addition. Moreover, it is apparent that it is possible to establish that an object's shadow equals it without any need for an addition. Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, stood alone among the scholars at large, saying: The time of Zuhr remains until the shadow becomes twice the object's length. Then, when it exceeds that by a little, it is the beginning of the time for 'Asr.

[p-284 continued] Al-Nawawi, in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*, quoted from al-Qadi Abu al-Tayyib that Ibn al-Mundhir said: No one said this except Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him. His evidence is the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with him and his father, that he heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: "Your duration compared with the nations before you is like the period between the 'Asr prayer and the setting of the sun. The People of the Torah were given the Torah and they acted upon it until midday, when they became unable (to continue), so they were given a qirat each. Then the People of the Gospel were given the Gospel, and they acted upon it until the 'Asr prayer, when they became unable, so they were given a qirat each. Then we were given the Qur'an, and we acted upon it until the sunset, and we were given two qirats each. The People of the Book said: 'Our Lord, You gave these two qirats each and gave us one qirat each, while we did more work!' God, the Exalted, said: (Has anything been withheld from your reward?) They said: No. He said: That is My bounty, which I give to whom I will." Agreed upon. He said: This is evidence that the time of 'Asr is shorter than the time of Zuhr. From the time the shadow of an object equals it until sunset is a quarter of the day, and it is not less than the time of Zuhr, but equal to it.

This line of evidence has been answered: the purpose of this hadith is to give an illustration, not to define the times of the prayers. The purpose of the hadiths indicating that the time of Zuhr ends when an object's shadow equals it is to define the times of the prayers. It has been established in the principles of jurisprudence that taking rulings from their proper sources is better than taking them from non-proper sources. Moreover, the hadith does not explicitly state that one of the two periods is longer than the other; it only says that their (the people's) work was greater. Greater work does not necessarily entail a greater duration of time, since some people may do much work in a short time. This is supported by the fact that this Ummah was relieved of the burdens and shackles that were upon them.

Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: Abu Hanifa opposed the reports and the people with this statement, and his own companions opposed him. When you have verified that the truth is that the beginning of the time of 'Asr is when the shadow of every object equals it, without considering the shadow at the time of zawal (the sun's zenith), then know that the end of the time of 'Asr is defined in some hadiths as when the shadow of every object becomes twice its length. In others it is defined as before the sun turns yellow, and in others its extension is until sunset. In the hadith of Jabir and Ibn 'Abbas, mentioned earlier concerning Jibril's leading of the prayer, in his explanation of the end of the time of 'Asr on the second day: then he prayed 'Asr when the shadow of every object was twice its length. In the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, and in (the narration) of Muslim and Ahmad: "The time of the 'Asr prayer is as long as the sun has not turned yellow." In the hadith of Abu Musa in (the collections of) Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i: then he delayed 'Asr, and he departed from it while the one speaking would say: the sun has turned red. Imam Ahmad, Muslim and the authors of the Four Sunan related similar from the hadith of Buraydah al-Aslami. In the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, and in (the narration) of Muslim: "The time of the 'Asr prayer is as long as the sun has not turned yellow and its first horn has not set."

In the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, agreed upon: "Whoever catches one rak'ah of 'Asr before the sun sets has caught 'Asr."

The apparent way of reconciling these narrations concerning the end of the time of 'Asr is that the point at which an object's shadow equals twice its length is the time when the sun changes from whiteness and clarity to yellowness. Thus the meanings of the two narrations return to one thing, as some Malikis have said.

Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni*: The scholars have agreed that whoever prays 'Asr while the sun is white and clear has prayed it within its time. In this there is evidence that observing the two-times (shadow) is, in their view, recommended, and perhaps the two (limits) are close, so that one is found near the other. End of quotation, in his own words. This is the end of its preferred (ikhtiyari) time.

As for the narrations indicating that its time extends until sunset, they apply to those with valid excuses, such as a menstruating woman who becomes pure, a disbeliever who embraces Islam, a child who reaches puberty, a madman who regains sanity, a sleeper who wakes, and a sick person who recovers. This reconciliation is supported by what Imam Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i related from the hadith of Anas, who said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: "That is the prayer of the hypocrite: he sits watching the sun until it is between the two horns of Satan, then he rises and pecks at it four times, remembering God only a little." In this hadith there is evidence that it is not permissible to delay the 'Asr prayer until the sun turns yellow or beyond, without an excuse.

* *

The beginning of the time for the Maghrib prayer is the sunset, that is, the disappearance of the disc of the sun, by the consensus of the Muslims. In the hadith of Jabir and Ibn 'Abbas concerning Jibril's leading of the prayer: "Then he prayed Maghrib when the sun set." In the hadith of Salamah ibn al-Akwa', may God be pleased with him, that the Messenger of God ﷺ "used to pray Maghrib when the sun set and was hidden by the veil." Reported by the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), Imam Ahmad, and the authors of the Four Sunan except al-Nasa'i. The hadiths on this are numerous.

The end of its time, that is, of Maghrib, has been disputed. Some scholars said: It has only one time, which is the amount of time in which it can be prayed at its beginning, while observing its conditions. This was said by al-Shafi'i, and it is the well-known position of Malik. The evidence of the proponents of this view is that Jibril led the Prophet ﷺ in prayer on the second night at the same time he had prayed it on the first, and they said: If it had another time, he would have delayed it to that time on the second night, as he did with all the other prayers.

The correct view is that the time of Maghrib extends as long as the twilight (shafaq) has not disappeared. Muslim in his *Sahih* related from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, mentioned earlier, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "And the time of Maghrib is as long as the glow (thawr) of the twilight has not set," the hadith in full. The meaning of thawr al-shafaq is its spreading, its spread and its main body. In the Qamus, it is said that it is the red glow of the twilight that spreads in it. In the hadith of Abu Musa mentioned earlier in (the collections of) Ahmad and Muslim, and the hadith of Buraydah mentioned earlier in (the collections of) Ahmad, Muslim and the Four Sunan: "Then he delayed Maghrib until the twilight had set." In one wording: "Then he prayed Maghrib before the twilight had set."

As for the answer to the hadiths of Jibril's leading of the prayer, where he prayed Maghrib on both days at one time, it has three aspects:

First: He limited himself to explaining the preferred time and did not encompass the permissible time. This applies to all prayers except Zuhr.

Second: That (Jibril's leading) was earlier, at the beginning of the matter in Makkah, whereas these hadiths about the extension of the time of Maghrib until the disappearance of the twilight are later, at the end of the matter in Madinah, so it is obligatory to rely on them.

Third: These hadiths are more authentic in their chain than the hadith of Jibril's explanation, so they must be given priority. This was said by al-Shawkani, may God have mercy on him. There is no disagreement among the scholars about the excellence of hastening the Maghrib prayer at the beginning of its time. The school of Imam Malik, may God have mercy on him, holds that the emergency time for Maghrib extends, in shared (time) with 'Isha', until Fajr.

Al-Bayhaqi said in *al-Sunan al-Kubra*: We have related from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf concerning a woman who becomes pure before the rising of dawn that she prays Maghrib and 'Isha. The apparent evidence for this view, which extends the emergency time for Maghrib until the rising of dawn as is the position of Malik, is what is also established in the authentic (collections) that the Prophet ﷺ "combined Maghrib and 'Isha in Madinah without fear or travel." Al-Bukhari and Muslim in their *Sahihs* related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that "the Prophet ﷺ prayed in Madinah seven and eight: Zuhr, 'Asr, Maghrib and 'Isha." Its meaning is that he prayed the seven together in one time, and the eight likewise, as is clarified by al-Bukhari's narration in the chapter on "the time of Maghrib," from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ prayed seven together and eight together."

In a wording in Muslim, Ahmad and the authors of the Sunan except Ibn Majah: "He combined Zuhr and 'Asr, and Maghrib and 'Isha, in Madinah without fear or rain." It was said to Ibn 'Abbas: What did he intend by that? He said: He intended not to burden his Ummah. By this you know that the statement of Malik in the *Muwatta'* that "perhaps that was due to the cause of rain" is not correct.

In the wording of most narrations: "without fear or travel." We have already stated that this combination must be understood as an apparent (surface) combination, because it is established in the principles that combination is obligatory when possible. By this interpretation the hadiths are harmonized and there is no contradiction between them. Among what shows that this interpretation is required is what al-Nasa'i related "from Ibn 'Abbas, in the wording: 'I prayed with the Prophet ﷺ Zuhr and 'Asr together, and Maghrib and 'Isha together: he delayed Zuhr and hastened 'Asr, and delayed Maghrib and hastened 'Isha.'" So this Ibn 'Abbas, the narrator of the hadith of combination, has explicitly stated that what he related of the said combination is the apparent combination.
