Thus al-Nasa'i's narration is explicit on the point of dispute and clarifies the ambiguity present in the said combination.

It has been established in the principles that clarification by means of a report whose chain is weaker than the chain of the thing clarified is permissible according to the majority of the scholars of jurisprudence, as well as the hadith scholars. He alluded to this in *Maraqi al-Su'ud* in the section on clarification, with his verse (rajaz):

"And a deficient (report) in chain or in indication clarified what is relied upon."

This is supported by what al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) related from 'Umar and Ibn Dinar, that he said: "O Abu al-Sha'tha', I think he delayed Zuhr and hastened 'Asr, and delayed Maghrib and hastened 'Isha." He said: "And I too think so." Abu al-Sha'tha' is the narrator of the hadith from Ibn 'Abbas, and the narrator knows better what he narrated than others, because he may know from the context of the speech indications that the absent one does not know.

If it is said: It is established in the *Sahih of al-Bukhari* and elsewhere that Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani said to Abu al-Sha'tha': "Perhaps that combination was on a rainy night." Abu al-Sha'tha' said: "Perhaps."

The apparent answer, and God knows best, is that we do not claim that Abu al-Sha'tha' was certain of that, and the narration of the two Shaykhs from him is by way of supposition. Supposition does not preclude the possibility of the opposite, and that opposite possibility is what he meant by "perhaps." And God knows best.

What also supports this combination being an apparent combination is that Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them, both are among those from whom the said combination was narrated in Madinah, yet each of them also narrated from the Prophet ﷺ what indicates that the said combination means the apparent combination.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 103 (part 3 of 7):

As for Ibn Mas'ud, al-Tabarani narrated it from him, as Ibn Hajar mentioned in *Fath al-Bari*. (p-288) Al-Shawkani said in *Nayl al-Awtar*: al-Tabarani narrated it from Ibn Mas'ud in *al-Kabir* and *al-Awsat*, as al-Haythami mentioned in *Majma' al-Zawa'id*, with the wording: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ combined the Zuhr and the 'Asr, and combined the Maghrib and the 'Isha'. He was asked about that, and he said: 'I did that so that my community would not be burdened.'" However, Malik in *al-Muwatta'*, al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud and al-Nasa'i narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "I never saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ pray a prayer outside its appointed time except two prayers: he combined the Maghrib and the 'Isha' at Muzdalifah, and he prayed the Fajr that day before its appointed time." Ibn Mas'ud's negation of the aforementioned combining indicates that the combining narrated from him is the formal combining (*jam' suri*, combining in appearance only), because each of the two prayers was performed in its own time; otherwise his statement would be contradictory. Combining is obligatory whenever it is possible.

As for Ibn 'Umar, 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated from him the aforementioned combining in Medina, as al-Shawkani also said, although Ibn Jarir narrated from him that he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ came out to us, and he would delay the Zuhr and hasten the 'Asr, and combine them; and he would delay the Maghrib and hasten the 'Isha', and combine them." Al-Shawkani also said this. This is the formal combining, and these narrations specify the meaning of the word *jama'a* (he combined).

Know that the word *jama'a* is a verb in an affirmative context, and the scholars of usul (legal theory) have established that an affirmative verb is not general across its types.

Ibn al-Hajib said in his *Mukhtasar al-Usuli*, in the section on the general (*al-'amm*), the following text: "An affirmative verb is not general across its types, such as *sallā dākhila al-Ka'bah* (he prayed inside the Ka'bah), so it does not cover the obligatory and the voluntary prayer..." up to his saying: "And *kāna yajma'u bayna al-ṣalātayn* (he used to combine between the two prayers) does not cover their two times. As for the repetition of the action, it is derived from the narrator's statement *kāna yajma'u* (he used to combine), like their saying *kāna Hatim yukrimu al-ḍayf* (Hatim used to honour the guest)..." etc.

His commentator al-'Adud said the following text: "When one says *kāna yajma'u bayna al-ṣalatayn al-zuhr wa al-'asr, wa al-maghrib wa al-'isha'* (he used to combine the two prayers, Zuhr and 'Asr, and Maghrib and 'Isha'), their combining does not generalise to the combining by advancing in the time of the first prayer and delaying in the time of the second. Its generality in time does not indicate this either, and it may be mistakenly thought to, from his saying *kāna yaf'alu* (he used to do), since repetition is understood from it, as when one says *kāna Hatim yukrimu al-ḍayf*. But this is not among what we have mentioned at all, because it is not understood from the verb (*yajma'u*) but from the narrator's statement, which is *kāna*. Even if he had said *jama'a* (he combined), the misconception would have disappeared." The end of the point of interest from his words, with slight omission of what is not needed for our purpose. His statement "Even if he had said *jama'a*, the misconception would have disappeared" indicates that Ibn 'Abbas's statement in the aforementioned hadith, *jama'a*, is not understood as general. Accordingly, no particular form of combining is determined except by a separate (*munfasil*) proof. (p-289)

We have already presented the evidence that the intended combining is the formal combining.

The author of *Jam' al-Jawami'*, listing what does not indicate generality, said the following text: "An affirmative verb, such as *kāna yajma'u fi al-safar* (he used to combine during travel)."

His commentator, the author of *al-Diya' al-Lami'*, said the following text: "*Nahwa kāna yajma'u fi al-safar*, i.e., between the Zuhr and the 'Asr, and the Maghrib and the 'Isha', it has no generality either, because it is a verb in an affirmative context. So their combining does not cover advancing in the time of the first and delaying until the time of the second." Al-Rahuni explained Ibn al-Hajib's words in this way, up to his saying: "The author singled out this last verb for mention, although it is a verb in an affirmative context, because *kāna* has an additional meaning, namely that it requires repetition by custom when combined with the present tense, so generality may be mistakenly inferred from it, as in *kāna Hatim yukrimu al-ḍiyfān* (Hatim used to honour the guests)."

Al-Fihri and al-Rahuni stated this explicitly. Wali al-Din reported from the Imam (al-Razi) in *al-Mahsul* that it does not, by custom or linguistically, require repetition.

* *

Wali al-Din said: "A verb in an affirmative context does not generalise, like an indefinite affirmative noun, unless it occurs in the context of enumerating favours (*al-imtinan*), as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We sent down from the sky pure water﴾ [al-Furqan: 48]." End of quotation from *al-Diya' al-Lami'* of Ibn Halawlaw.

The one who wrote this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: The reason that an affirmative verb does not generalise is that, according to the grammarians and some rhetoricians, the verb is analysed into a verbal noun (*masdar*) and a tense (*zaman*); and according to a group of rhetoricians it is analysed into a verbal noun, a tense and an attribution (*nisbah*). The verbal noun is implicit in its meaning by consensus, and the verbal noun implicit in it is not made definite by any definiter, so it is indefinite in meaning. It is known that an indefinite does not generalise in affirmation, and this is the view of the majority of scholars. As for what some of them claim, that the formal combining did not occur in the speech of the Lawgiver (the Prophet ﷺ) or in the speech of the people of his time, this is rejected by what we have presented earlier from Ibn 'Abbas in al-Nasa'i and from Ibn 'Umar in 'Abd al-Razzaq, and by what Abu Dawud, Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi (who authenticated it), al-Shafi'i, Ibn Majah, al-Daraqutni and al-Hakim narrated from the hadith of Hamnah bint Jahsh, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet ﷺ said to her when she was suffering from *istihadah* (irregular bleeding): "If you are able to delay the Zuhr and hasten the 'Asr, then perform *ghusl* (ritual bath) and pray the Zuhr and the 'Asr together; then delay the Maghrib and hasten the 'Isha', then perform *ghusl* and combine the two prayers, and do so; and perform *ghusl* with the Fajr." (p-290) He said: "This is the more pleasing of the two matters to me." Among what indicates that the combining mentioned in the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas is formal combining is what al-Nasa'i narrated through 'Amr ibn Harim from Abu al-Sha'tha'," that Ibn 'Abbas prayed in Basra the Zuhr and the 'Asr with nothing between them, and the Maghrib and the 'Isha' with nothing between them; he did this because of an engagement (*shughl*)," and it contains his raising it to the Prophet ﷺ. In a narration of Muslim through 'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq, the engagement of Ibn 'Abbas was the sermon (*khutbah*), and he delivered the sermon after the 'Asr prayer until the stars appeared; then he combined the Maghrib and the 'Isha'. In it is also confirmation by Abu Hurayrah of Ibn 'Abbas's raising of it. End of quotation from *Fath al-Bari*.

What al-Khattabi and Ibn Hajar in *al-Fath* mentioned, that the Prophet's ﷺ statement "I did that so that my community would not be burdened," in the two aforementioned hadiths of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, contradicts interpreting it as formal combining, because the intention behind it involves some burden, and that it is narrower than performing each prayer in its time, since the beginnings and ends of the times are difficult for the elite to perceive, let alone the common people, is answered by what the scholar al-Shawkani, may Allah have mercy on him, answered in *Nayl al-Awtar*. It is that the Lawgiver ﷺ had informed his community of the beginnings and ends of the times and emphasised the informing and the explanation, to the extent that he specified them by perceptible signs that hardly any common person, let alone the elite, could confuse. The relief lies in delaying one of the two prayers to the end of its time and performing the other at the beginning of its time, which is established in comparison with performing each of them at the beginning of its time, as was his ﷺ constant practice, to the extent that 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "He never prayed a prayer at the end of its time twice until Allah took him." No fair-minded person doubts that performing the two prayers at once and going out for them one time is lighter than performing each of them at the beginning of its time.

Among those who held that the aforementioned combining means formal combining are Ibn al-Majishun, al-Tahawi, Imam al-Haramayn and al-Qurtubi. Ibn Sayyid al-Nas strengthened it by what we have presented earlier from Abu al-Sha'tha'. Al-Nawawi somewhat inclined to it in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*, in the chapter on the times (*al-mawaqit*) in the Book of Prayer.

If it is said: The formal combining to which you have attributed the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas is performing each of the two combined prayers in its own time, and this is not a concession (*rukhsah*), but an obligatory default (*'azimah*). So what is the benefit then in the Prophet's ﷺ statement "so that my community would not be burdened," given that the hadiths specifying the times include the formal combining? And is interpreting the combining as covered by the hadiths on the timings anything other than discarding its benefit and nullifying its content? The answer is what the scholar al-Shawkani, may Allah have mercy on him, also answered: there is no doubt that the statements issued from him ﷺ in the hadiths on the timing of the prayers include the formal combining, as the objector mentioned. So it is not correct that the lifting of hardship is attributed to them; rather it is attributed to the actions alone, for what we have made you aware of, namely that he ﷺ never prayed a prayer at the end of its time twice. So someone might think that performing the prayer at the beginning of its time is binding, because he ﷺ constantly did so throughout his life. Therefore, in his combining there was a formal combining that brought ease and facilitation for whoever followed merely by the action.

The Companions followed actions more than statements. For this reason, the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, refrained from slaughtering their sacrificial camels on the day of al-Hudaybiyah after he ﷺ had commanded them to slaughter, until he ﷺ entered upon Umm Salamah distressed. She advised him to slaughter and to call the barber to shave for him, so he did. Then they all slaughtered, and they nearly perished from grief because of the crowding of some of them upon others during the shaving. What further supports that the disputed combining is not permitted without an excuse is what al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Whoever combines between the two prayers without an excuse has committed one of the major sins (*abwab al-kaba'ir*)." In its chain is Hanash ibn Qays, who is weak.

Among what also indicates this is what al-Tirmidhi said at the end of his *Sunan*, in the Book of Defects (*kitab al-'ilal*) of it. His words are: "All of what is in this book of mine of hadith is acted upon, and some of the people of knowledge have taken by it, except two hadiths: the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, that the Prophet ﷺ combined the Zuhr and the 'Asr in Medina, and the Maghrib and the 'Isha', without fear or travel," etc. From this you know that al-Tirmidhi says that none of the people of knowledge went to act upon this hadith regarding combining by advancing or delaying. So nothing remains except the formal combining, and it is determined.

The one who wrote this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: It has been narrated from a group of the people of knowledge that they permitted combining while resident (*fi al-hadar*) for need, absolutely, but on condition that it not become a habit. Among them are Ibn Sirin, Rabi'ah, Ashhab, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Qaffal al-Kabir.

Al-Khattabi related it from a group of the people of hadith. Ibn Hajar and others said: their evidence is what preceded in the hadith, his saying: "so that my community would not be burdened." You have known from what preceded that the evidence determines that this be interpreted as formal combining, as mentioned. And Allah knows best.

* *

Note (tanbih)

It has become clear from these proofs that we have presented that the Zuhr has no time extending to sunset, and that the Maghrib has no time extending to dawn. However, this excluded time indicated by the proofs (p-292) must be interpreted as the preferred time (*al-waqt al-ikhtiyari*), so it does not contradict the extension of the Zuhr's necessity time (*al-waqt al-darury*) to sunset, and the Maghrib's necessity time to dawn, as Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said, because of the proofs establishing the sharing of the Zuhr and 'Asr in time under necessity, and likewise the Maghrib and 'Isha'. The clearest proof of this is the permissibility of both combining by advancing (*jam' al-taqdim*) and combining by delaying (*jam' al-ta'khir*) while travelling. Praying the 'Asr together with the Zuhr at the sun's decline is evidence of their sharing a time under necessity, and praying the Zuhr after its time has elapsed, within the time of the 'Asr in combining by delaying, is evidence of their sharing that time under necessity as well. The same applies to the Maghrib and 'Isha'. As for combining by delaying in such a way that one prays the Zuhr in the time of the 'Asr and the Maghrib in the time of the 'Isha', this is established in the agreed-upon narrations. Al-Bukhari in his *Sahih* narrated from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When the Prophet ﷺ set out before the sun declined, he would delay the Zuhr until the time of the 'Asr, then he would combine them both."

Ibn Hajar said in his commentary on this hadith: "His words, 'then he combines them,' meaning at the time of ʿAṣr. In Qutayba's narration from al-Mufaddal, in the chapter that follows, it says: 'Then he descended and combined them.' Muslim has, from the narration of Jabir ibn Isma'il, from ʿUqayl: 'He delays Ẓuhr until the time of ʿAṣr, then combines them, and delays Maghrib until he combines it with ʿIshā' when the twilight (al-shafaq) disappears.' He also has, from the narration of Shababa, from ʿUqayl: 'until the beginning of the time of ʿAṣr enters, then he combines them.'" End of quotation. From him, in his exact words.

In the two Ṣaḥīḥs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with them both), that the Prophet (ﷺ) "when travelling quickened his journey, combined Maghrib and ʿIshā'." This combining cannot be understood as jam' al-ṣūrī (the merely formal combining, in which each prayer is performed at its own time with the two placed side by side). This is because the sound narrations we mentioned just above explicitly state that he prayed Ẓuhr at the time of ʿAṣr, and Maghrib after the disappearance of the twilight.

Al-Bayhaqi said in al-Sunan al-Kubra: The narrations of Yahya ibn Saʿid al-Ansari, Musa ibn ʿUqba, ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿUmar, Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, and Umar ibn Muhammad ibn Zayd, from Nafiʿ, agree that Ibn ʿUmar's combining of the two prayers took place after the disappearance of the twilight. Those who opposed them, and who are not comparable to them in preserving the hadiths of Nafiʿ, differed. Then, shortly after this, he said: The narrations of the memorisers (al-huffaz) among Nafiʿ's students are more deserving of being correct. Salim ibn ʿAbd Allah, Aslam the freedman of ʿUmar, ʿAbd Allah ibn Dinar, and Isma'il ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Dhu'ayb (it is also said: Ibn Dhu'ayb) narrated from Ibn ʿUmar in agreement with their narration. Then al-Bayhaqi cited the chains (asanid) of their narrations.

As for jam' al-taqdim (combining by advancing), in which ʿAṣr is prayed at the time of the sun's decline together with Ẓuhr at the beginning of its time, and ʿIshā' together with Maghrib at the setting of the sun at the beginning of its time, this is (p. 293) also established from the Prophet (ﷺ), even though some scholars denied it and tried to weaken its hadiths. Many hadiths have come from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning it, some of which are sound and some of which are fair (ḥasan).

Among them is what Muslim included in his Ṣaḥīḥ from the long hadith of Jabir concerning the Ḥajj: "Then he gave the adhan, then the iqama, and prayed Ẓuhr; then he gave the iqama and prayed ʿAṣr, and did not pray anything between them." This took place after the sun's decline. This is a sound hadith, which explicitly states that he prayed ʿAṣr early, together with Ẓuhr, after the sun's decline.

Abu Dawud, Ahmad, and al-Tirmidhi (who said: "fair, gharib") and Ibn Hibban, al-Daraqutni, al-Bayhaqi, and al-Hakim narrated from Muʿadh (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet (ﷺ) "was on the expedition of Tabuk: when he set off before the sun declined, he delayed Ẓuhr until he combined it with ʿAṣr, praying them both together, and then he continued his journey. When he set off after the sun declined, he prayed Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr together, then he travelled on. And when he set off before Maghrib, he delayed Maghrib until he prayed it with ʿIshā'; and when he set off after Maghrib, he hastened ʿIshā' and prayed it with Maghrib." Rejecting jam' al-taqdim by weakening this hadith, as al-Hakim and Ibn Hazm attempted, is of no consequence, because of what you have seen just above: that jam' al-taqdim is recorded by Muslim in his Ṣaḥīḥ from the long hadith of Jabir. Also from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), from the Prophet (ﷺ): "that when travelling, if the sun declined while he was at his stopping place, he combined Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr before mounting. If the sun had not declined while he was at his stopping place, he travelled on until, when the time of ʿAṣr arrived, he dismounted and combined Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr. And when the time of Maghrib arrived while he was at his stopping place, he combined it with ʿIshā'; and if the time had not arrived while he was at his stopping place, he rode until, when it was time for ʿIshā', he dismounted and combined them." Ahmad narrated it. Al-Shafiʿi narrated something similar in his Musnad, and in it: "If he set out before the sun declined, he delayed Ẓuhr until he combined it with ʿAṣr at the time of ʿAṣr." Al-Bayhaqi and al-Daraqutni narrated it too. It is also reported from al-Tirmidhi that he graded it as fair (ḥasan).

If it is said: The hadith of Muʿadh is flawed (maʿlūl) because Qutayba is alone in narrating it against the memorisers; because it is mu'an'an (narrated with "ʿan," "from") from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, from Abu al-Tufayl, and no hearing (samāʿ) from him by Yazid is known, as Ibn Hazm stated; and because its chain includes Abu al-Tufayl, who is criticised for having been the standard-bearer of al-Mukhtar ibn Abi ʿUbayd, and who believed in the return (al-rajʿa); and because al-Hakim said: "it is fabricated (mawḍūʿ)"; and because Abu Dawud said: "there is no established hadith concerning jam' al-taqdim"; and because the hadith of Ibn ʿAbbas has in its chain Husayn ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, who is weak, then the answer is that the claim that it is flawed by Qutayba's sole narration is rejected for two reasons:

The first: Qutayba ibn Saʿid (may Allah have mercy on him), with his well-known standing in justice (ʿadāla), precision (ḍabṭ) and mastery (itqān), did not differ from others in this narration; rather, he added what others did not mention. The one who memorised is a proof against the one who did not memorise. It is established in the science of hadith that the additions (ziyādāt) of trustworthy narrators are accepted, especially since this addition, which is jam' al-taqdim, has already been established in Muslim's Ṣaḥīḥ from the hadith of Jabir, and it will come, God willing, that it is also authentic from the hadith of Anas.

The second reason: Qutayba was not alone in narrating it, for al-Mufaddal ibn Faḍāla followed him in it. Ibn al-Qayyim said in Zad al-Maʿad, and his words are: "Abu Dawud narrated it from Yazid ibn Khalid ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn Mawhab al-Ramli: al-Mufaddal ibn Faḍāla narrated to us, from al-Layth ibn Saʿd, from Hisham ibn Saʿd, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Abu al-Tufayl, from Muʿadh, and he mentioned it." So this al-Mufaddal followed Qutayba, although Qutayba is greater than al-Mufaddal and more retentive; but Qutayba's solitary narration is thereby removed. End of quotation. From him, in his exact words.

Al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Sunan al-Kubra. He said: Abu ʿAli al-Rudhbari informed us, Abu Bakr ibn Dasa informed us, Abu Dawud narrated to us; then he cited the chain mentioned just above, namely the chain of Abu Dawud which Ibn al-Qayyim cited. The text in it explicitly states jam' al-taqdim. Likewise al-Nasa'i and al-Daraqutni narrated it, as Ibn Hajar said in al-Talkhis. Thus it became clear that Qutayba did not stand alone in this hadith, because Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, al-Daraqutni and al-Bayhaqi all brought it out by another route, as a follow-up (mutābaʿa) to Qutayba's narration.

Ibn Hajar said in al-Takhlīṣ: In the chain of this route is Hisham ibn Saʿd, who is "lenient in hadith" (layyin al-ḥadīth).

Its compiler, may Allah pardon him, says: Hisham ibn Saʿd mentioned is among the narrators of Muslim, and al-Bukhari cited him in suspended form (taʿlīq). Through this you know the soundness of al-Mufaddal's route as a follow-up to Qutayba's route. For this reason al-Bayhaqi said in al-Sunan al-Kubra: The Shaykh said: "They only rejected from this the narration of Yazid ibn Abi Habib from Abu al-Tufayl. As for the narration of Abu al-Zubayr from Abu al-Tufayl, it is preserved and sound." Know that it is not hidden that what is related from al-Bukhari, may Allah have mercy on him, that he asked Qutayba about the one who wrote this hadith with him from al-Layth ibn Saʿd, and he said: "Khalid al-Madaʾini wrote it with me." Al-Bukhari said: "Khalid al-Madaʾini used to insert into the narrations of the shaykhs (yudkhilu ʿalā al-shuyūkh), meaning he inserted into their narrations what was not part of them." This does not show that it is a defect in Qutayba's narration, because a trustworthy and precise narrator is not harmed by taking the thousands of liars along with him, since he only narrates what he knows, and the lying of others does not harm him, as is evident.

As for the answer to what Ibn Hazm said, that it is mu'an'an from Yazid ibn Abi Habib from Abu al-Tufayl, and no hearing from him is known, there are two answers:

The first: the ʿanʿana (narration with "from") and similar expressions have, in the view of the scholars of hadith, the ruling of an explicit statement of transmission (taḥdīth), unless the one using ʿanʿana is a mudallis (one who conceals defects, practising tadlīs). Yazid ibn Abi Habib: al-Dhahabi said of him in Tadhkirat al-Huffāẓ: "He was a proof, a memoriser of hadith," and he mentioned among those from whom he narrated Abu al-Tufayl mentioned. Ibn Hajar said of him in al-Taqrīb: "trustworthy, a jurist, and he used to send (yursil) narrations." It is known that irsāl (sending a hadith with a missing link) is not the same as tadlīs, because irsāl in the terminology of the hadith scholars is a Successor (tābiʿī), or a senior Successor in particular, raising a hadith directly to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is also said: the omission of a narrator in general, which is the view of the jurists (uṣūliyyūn). So irsāl is a severed (maqṭūʿ) narration in which the intermediary is dropped, unlike tadlīs. In tadlīs of the chain, the narrator drops his immediate shaykh and attributes the narration to the shaykh of his shaykh, a contemporary, using a term that may indicate hearing directly or through an intermediary, such as "from so-and-so" or "so-and-so said." In this case he does not definitively deny an intermediary; rather, it creates the impression of continuity, because there must be contemporaneity between him and the one to whom he attributes it, meaning the shaykh of his shaykh; otherwise it would be disconnected (munqaṭiʿ), as is well known in the sciences of hadith. Ibn Hazm's statement that no hearing from him is known is not a defect, because contemporaneity is sufficient, and it is not a condition that meeting (liqāʾ) be established, much less that hearing be established. Muslim ibn al-Ḥajjāj does not stipulate in his Ṣaḥīḥ anything more than contemporaneity, so he does not stipulate meeting, much less hearing. Al-Bukhari alone stipulated meeting. Al-ʿIraqi said in his Alfiyya:

"They deemed the connection of the ʿanʿana sound, if it is free of the concealment of its narrator and meeting is known;
and some related this as a consensus, but Muslim did not stipulate the meeting, only contemporaneity..."

[The verses continue; the rest of the text follows.]

In sum, the consensus of the Muslims on the soundness of Muslim's hadiths is not hidden, although he only stipulated contemporaneity. Through this you know that the statement of Ibn Hazm and those who agreed with him, that the narration of Yazid ibn Abi Habib from Abu al-Tufayl is not known, does not undermine his hadith, because of what you have learned: that ʿanʿana from a non-mudallis has the ruling of transmission. Yazid ibn Abi Habib died in the year 128 AH, and he was close to eighty years old.

Abu al-Tufayl was born in the year of Uhud and died in the year 110 AH according to the sound view. Through this you know there is no doubt about their contemporaneity and their coexistence in life for a long period. There is no marvel in Ibn Hazm's ruling that the narration of Yazid ibn Abi Habib from Abu al-Tufayl is invalid, for he committed something worse in his ruling on the established hadith in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhari: "There will certainly be among my nation peoples who consider as permissible the silk (ḥarīr), the wine (khamr), and the musical instruments (maʿāzif)," by saying that it is not connected and cannot be used as proof because al-Bukhari said at the beginning of the chain: "Hisham ibn ʿAmmar said." It is known that Hisham ibn ʿAmmar was one of al-Bukhari's teachers, and that al-Bukhari was very far from tadlīs. To the refutation of this against Ibn Hazm, al-Iraqi alluded in his Alfiyya with his words:

"If the first part of the chain is dropped along with the form of definite statement, it is known as taʿlīq (suspended);
and if the whole chain is dropped, what he attributed to his shaykh with 'qāla' is like that;
an ʿanʿana like the hadith of the musical instruments: do not listen to Ibn Hazm the dissenter."

Although what is known from Malik, Ahmad and Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on them) is the acceptance of the mursal (a narration where the Successor attributes directly to the Prophet, omitting the Companion), and the mursal in the terminology of the jurists is what has any narrator dropped from it. So in the jurists' terminology it includes the munqaṭiʿ and the muʿḍal. It is known that whoever accepts the mursal accepts the ʿanʿana of the mudallis all the more, as more than one scholar has stated, and this is clear. The answer to the criticism of Abu al-Tufayl, that he was the standard-bearer of al-Mukhtar, is rejected for two reasons:

The first: Abu al-Tufayl was a Companion (ṣaḥābī), and he was the last of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to die, as Muslim said, and as the author of ʿAmūd al-Nasab set out in his verse:

"The last of the Companions to die was for him Abu al-Tufayl, ʿĀmir ibn Wāthila."

This Abu al-Tufayl is ʿĀmir ibn Wāthila ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn Jahsh al-Laythi, named after the Layth ibn Bakr ibn Kinana. All the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them all) are upright (ʿudūl), and their praise (tazkiya) has come in the Book of Allah and the Sunna of His Prophet (ﷺ), as is known in its proper place. The ruling that all the Companions are upright is the view of the majority, and it is the truth. Al-Ghazi (or the author) said in Marāqī al-Suʿūd:

"Other than them is a narration, and the Companions:
their praise is for all, to which all incline."

*(p-297)*

*Poem:*
"He chose, among those who constantly accompanied him, over one who saw him only once, an Imam who is trusted."

The second aspect is what al-Shawkani, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in *Nayl al-Awtar* (*Nayl al-Awtar*, "The Attainment of Objectives"): that Abu al-Tufayl only went out with al-Mukhtar (al-Mukhtar ibn Abi Ubayd al-Thaqafi) against the killers of al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with him, and that he did not know from al-Mukhtar that he believed in the *raj'ah* (the return of the dead to the world before the Resurrection). As for the answer to al-Hakim's claim that the hadith is *mawdu'* (fabricated), it is that this claim is not valid; rather, the hadith is authentic and is not fabricated.

Ibn al-Qayyim said: "His ruling that it is fabricated regarding this hadith is not accepted," meaning al-Hakim.

*(p-297)* Ibn al-Qayyim also said in *Zad al-Ma'ad* (*Zad al-Ma'ad*, "Provision for the Hereafter"): Al-Hakim said, "This hadith is fabricated, and its isnad (chain of narration) meets the conditions of the authentic (*sahih*), but it has been struck by a strange defect." Al-Hakim said: Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Balawayh narrated to us, Musa ibn Harun narrated to us, Qutaybah ibn Sa'id narrated to us, al-Layth ibn Sa'd narrated to us, from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, from Abu al-Tufayl, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, that the Prophet (ﷺ) "was on the expedition to Tabuk..." up to his saying: "And when he set off after the sun had declined, he prayed the Dhuhr and the 'Asr together, then he proceeded," and so on, the hadith.

Al-Hakim said: The narrators of this hadith are imams and trustworthy, and it is anomalous (*shadhdh*) in both its isnad and its text. Then we do not know any defect by which we could find fault with it. If the hadith were from al-Layth, from Abu al-Zubayr, from Abu al-Tufayl, we would have found fault with it because of that; and if it were from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, from Abu al-Tufayl, we would have found fault with it because of that. But since we do not find these two defects in it, it is no longer defective. Then we examined and did not find for Yazid ibn Abi Habib a narration from Abu al-Tufayl, nor did we find this text in this form from any of the companions of Abu al-Tufayl, nor from anyone who narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal other than Abu al-Tufayl. So we said: the hadith is anomalous. They narrated from Abu al-'Abbas al-Thaqafi, who said: Qutaybah ibn Sa'id used to say: "For us, concerning this hadith, there is the mark of Ahmad ibn Hanbal, 'Ali ibn al-Madini, Yahya ibn Ma'in, Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, and Abu Khaythamah," until Qutaybah counted seven of the imams of hadith who wrote this hadith from him. The imams of hadith only heard it from Qutaybah out of wonder at its isnad and text. Then it did not reach us that any of them mentioned a defect in the hadith. Then he said: "We examined it, and behold, the hadith is fabricated," while Qutaybah is trustworthy and reliable. End of quotation. The point of relevance is taken from it with slight paraphrase that does not affect any of the meaning. Consult it, for his saying "If it were from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, from Abu al-Tufayl, we would have found fault with it" implies that its isnad, which he cited, is from Yazid, from Abu al-Tufayl.

From this you know that al-Hakim's ruling that this hadith is fabricated has no basis. As for the men of its isnad, they are trustworthy by his own acknowledgment. We have already mentioned to you that Qutaybah was followed in it by al-Mufaddal ibn Fadalah, according to Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, al-Bayhaqi, and al-Daraqutni. The solitary narration of a trustworthy and precise (*dabit*) narrator of something no one else narrated is not considered an anomaly (*shudhudh*). How many authentic hadiths in the *Sahihayn* (the *Sahih* of al-Bukhari and Muslim) and elsewhere were transmitted by a single just and precise narrator alone! You have known that Qutaybah did not narrate it alone. As for its text, it is also far from anomaly.

We have already mentioned that the like of it was narrated by Muslim in his *Sahih* from Jabir, may Allah be pleased with him, and the like of it is also authentically reported from the hadith of Anas.

Ibn al-Qayyim said: Ishaq ibn Rahawayh narrated: Shababah narrated to us, al-Layth narrated to us, from 'Uqayl *(p-298)* from Ibn Shihab, from Anas, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "when he was on a journey and the sun declined, he prayed the Dhuhr and the 'Asr, then set off." This isnad is as you see. Shababah is Shababah ibn Sawwar, the trustworthy narrator whose hadith is agreed upon as evidence; Muslim narrated from him in his *Sahih*. So this isnad meets the conditions of al-Bukhari and Muslim (*al-Shaykhayn*). End of quotation, the relevant point taken verbatim.

Ibn Hajar said in *Fath al-Bari* (*Fath al-Bari*, "The Opening of the Creator's Work"), after citing the hadith of Ishaq, the following text: "It was given a defect by Ishaq's being solitary in narrating it from Shababah, and then by the solitary narration of Ja'far al-Firyabi from Ishaq. But that is not a disqualifying factor, for both are imams and memorizers (*huffaz*)." End of quotation, verbatim.

Al-Hakim narrated in *al-Arba'in* (*al-Arba'in*, "The Forty"), with a sahih isnad, from Anas, something similar to the hadith of Ishaq mentioned, and Abu Nu'aym has a similar narration in *Mustakhraj Muslim* (*Mustakhraj Muslim*, "Abu Nu'aym's extraction upon Muslim's Sahih"). The Hafiz said in *Bulugh al-Maram* (*Bulugh al-Maram*, "Attainment of the Objective"), after citing the hadith of Anas agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim), the following text: "In a narration of al-Hakim in *al-Arba'in* with a sahih isnad: 'He prayed the Dhuhr and the 'Asr, then rode,' and in Abu Nu'aym's *Mustakhraj Muslim*: 'When he was on a journey and the sun declined, he prayed the Dhuhr and the 'Asr together, then set off.'"

Ibn Hajar said in *Talkhis al-Habir* (*Talkhis al-Habir*, "Summary of al-Habir"), after citing al-Hakim's hadith with its isnad and text, the following text: "This is a strange addition (*ziyadah gharibah*), sahih in its isnad. Al-Mundhiri and al-'Ala'i authenticated it through this route. He marveled that al-Hakim did not include it in *al-Mustadrak* (*al-Mustadrak*, "The Supplement"). He said: It has another route narrated by al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat*," then he cited the hadith through it and said: "Ya'qub ibn Muhammad was solitary in it." What Ibn Hajar mentioned in *Fath* does not impair al-Hakim's narration here, namely that al-Bayhaqi cited al-Hakim's isnad, then mentioned the text without mentioning in it the addition of combining by advancing (*jam' al-taqdim*). This is because, as we have mentioned, one who memorized is a proof over one who did not memorize, and the addition of trustworthy narrators is accepted, as previously mentioned.

Al-Nawawi said in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab* (*Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*, "Commentary on al-Muhadhdhab"), after citing the hadith of Mu'adh which is our concern, the following text: "Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi narrated it, and he said: 'a good (*hasan*) hadith.'"

Al-Bayhaqi said: It is *mahfuz* (preserved) and sahih. And from Anas: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he was on a journey and the sun declined, prayed the Dhuhr and the 'Asr together, then set off." Narrated by al-Isma'ili and al-Bayhaqi with a sahih isnad.

Imam al-Haramayn said in *al-Asalib* (*al-Asalib*, "The Methods"): "Regarding the establishment of combining (*al-jam'*), there are sahih reports which are explicit texts that admit no interpretation. Its evidence in meaning is by inference from the consensus in its form, which is combining at 'Arafat and Muzdalifah, since it is not hidden that its cause is the need of the pilgrims for it because of their preoccupation with their rites, and this meaning exists in all journeys." End of quotation, the relevant point verbatim.

As for the response to the statement of Abu Dawud, "There is no established hadith regarding combining by advancing": what you have seen is that it is established in *Sahih Muslim* from the hadith of Jabir, and authentic from the hadith of Anas through the route of Ishaq ibn Rahawayh. Al-Hakim narrated it with a sahih isnad in *al-Arba'in*, Abu Nu'aym narrated it in *Mustakhraj Muslim*, and al-Isma'ili and al-Bayhaqi narrated it and said: "Its isnad is sahih," with the wording: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when he was on a journey and the sun declined, prayed the Dhuhr and the 'Asr together," up to the end of what preceded.

* *

Al-Shawkani said in *Nayl al-Awtar*: You have known that the hadiths on combining by advancing are partly sahih and partly good (*hasan*), and that refutes the statement of Abu Dawud, "There is no established hadith regarding combining by advancing." As for the answer to the weakening of the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas mentioned earlier regarding combining by advancing, on the grounds that its isnad contains Husayn ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, who is weak: it is that it was narrated through two other routes, by which the hadith is strengthened until its lowest rank becomes good (*hasan*).

The first: narrated by Yahya ibn 'Abd al-Hamid al-Hammani, from Abu Khalid al-Ahmar, from al-Hajjaj, from al-Hakam, from Miqsam, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second of them: narrated by Isma'il al-Qadi in *al-Ahkam* (*al-Ahkam*, "The Rulings"), from Isma'il ibn Abi Uways, from his brother, from Sulayman ibn Bilal, from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from Kurayb, from Ibn 'Abbas, with something similar. This was stated by Ibn Hajar in *Talkhis* and al-Shawkani in *Nayl al-Awtar*.

Ibn Hajar also said in *Talkhis*: It is said that al-Tirmidhi graded it good, and it seems he did so on the basis of corroboration (*mutabi'ah*). Ibn al-'Arabi erred and authenticated its isnad.

With all of this you know that both combining by advancing and combining by delaying during travel are established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that there is a form agreed upon in it, which is the one narrated by Muslim from Jabir in his lengthy hadith on the Hajj, as we have mentioned: combining by advancing at the midday prayer at 'Arafat, and combining by delaying at the night prayer at Muzdalifah.

Al-Bayhaqi said in *al-Sunan al-Kubra* (*al-Sunan al-Kubra*, "The Major Sunan"): Combining between the two prayers because of the excuse of travel is one of the well-known practices used among the Companions and the Followers, may Allah be pleased with them all, together with what is established from the Prophet (ﷺ), then from his Companions, then what the Muslims agreed upon regarding gathering people at 'Arafat and then at Muzdalifah. End of quotation, verbatim.

Al-Bayhaqi also narrated in *al-Sunan al-Kubra* from al-Zuhri that he asked Salim ibn 'Abd Allah: "Is it permissible to combine the Dhuhr and the 'Asr during travel?" He said: "Yes, there is no harm in that. Have you not seen the people's prayer at 'Arafat?" End of quotation, verbatim.

Ibn al-Qayyim said in *Zad al-Ma'ad*: Ibn Taymiyyah said: Combining by advancing is indicated by his combining at 'Arafat between the Dhuhr and the 'Asr, for the benefit of standing (in supplication), so that the time of supplication would be continuous and not be interrupted by descending for the 'Asr prayer, even though that was possible without hardship. So combining in this manner for the sake of hardship and need is more appropriate.

Al-Shafi'i said: What was most gentle for him on the day of 'Arafat was advancing the 'Asr, so that his supplication would be continuous and not interrupted by the 'Asr prayer. And delaying was gentler at Muzdalifah, so that his travel would be continuous and not interrupted by descending for the Maghrib, because of the constriction upon people in that. End of quotation from *Zad al-Ma'ad*.

So from these proofs we have presented in this discussion, you know that the 'Asr shares its time with the Dhuhr when necessity requires it, that the 'Isha' shares its time with the Maghrib when necessity requires it, that the Dhuhr shares its time with the 'Asr when necessity requires it, and that the Maghrib shares its time with the 'Isha' when necessity requires it, also. It is not hidden that the imams who disagreed with Malik, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, regarding the extension of the time of necessity for the Dhuhr until sunset, and the extension of the time of necessity for the Maghrib until dawn, such as al-Shafi'i and Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on both of them, and those who agree with them, are in reality in agreement with him, because they acknowledge that a menstruating woman who becomes pure before sunset by one rak'ah must pray the Dhuhr and the 'Asr together, and likewise if she becomes pure before dawn by one rak'ah she must pray the Maghrib and the 'Isha' together, as we have mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas and 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf. For if the time had completely expired, she would not be obliged to pray the Dhuhr or the Maghrib, by consensus that a menstruating woman does not make up prayers whose time expired while she was menstruating.

Al-Nawawi said in *Sharh al-Muhadhdhab*: We have mentioned that the sound position in our school is that the excused person is obliged to pray the Dhuhr with that which makes the 'Asr obligatory. This was said by 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Ibn 'Abbas, the seven jurists of Madinah, Ahmad, and others.

Al-Hasan, Hammad, Qatadah, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifah, Malik, and Dawud said: It is not obligatory for him. End of quotation, verbatim. Malik makes it obligatory to the extent that one could pray the first of the two shared times with one rak'ah remaining: that is four for the Maghrib and the 'Isha', and five for the Dhuhr and the 'Asr for the resident, and three for the traveler.

Ibn Qudamah said in *al-Mughni* (*al-Mughni*, "The Sufficient"): And this view was narrated, namely that one attains the Dhuhr, for example, by what one attains the 'Asr with, *(p-301)* in the case of a menstruating woman who becomes pure, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, Ibn 'Abbas, Tawus, Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, al-Zuhri, Rabi'ah, Malik, al-Layth, al-Shafi'i, Ishaq, and Abu Thawr.

Imam Ahmad said: Most of the Successors (tabi'un) hold this view, except al-Hasan alone, who said: "Only the prayer that becomes pure (from menstruation) within its time is obligatory, and that alone..." up to his saying: "Our evidence is what al-Athram, Ibn al-Mundhir and others narrated with their chains of transmission from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf and 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, that they both said concerning a menstruating woman who becomes pure one rak'ah before dawn: she prays Maghrib and 'Isha'. And if she becomes pure before the sun sets, she prays Zuhr and 'Asr together. Also, the time of the second prayer is the time of the first prayer during the state of excuse; so when the one with the excuse reaches it, the obligation of the first prayer falls upon her just as the obligation of the second prayer falls upon her." End of quotation from him in his own words with slight omission. This is an explicit statement from this great Hanbali scholar that the time of necessity (waqt al-darurah) for Maghrib extends until dawn, and for Zuhr until sunset, like the view of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him.

As for the beginning of the time of 'Isha', the Muslims have agreed that it enters when the twilight (ash-shafaq) disappears.

In the hadith of Jabir and Ibn 'Abbas, mentioned earlier, concerning Gabriel leading the Prophet in prayer, which explains the beginning of the time of 'Isha': then he prayed 'Isha' when the twilight had disappeared.

In the hadith of Buraydah mentioned earlier, in Muslim and others: then he commanded him, and he established 'Isha' when the twilight had disappeared.

In the hadith of Abu Musa in Muslim and others: then he commanded him, and he established 'Isha' when the twilight had disappeared. The hadiths with this meaning are very numerous, and this is a matter on which there is no dispute.

Since you now know the consensus of the scholars that the beginning of the time of 'Isha' is the disappearance of the twilight, know that the scholars differed concerning the meaning of ash-shafaq. Some scholars said: it is the redness (al-humrah), and this is the truth. Others said: it is the whiteness that follows the redness.

Among what indicates that ash-shafaq is the redness is what al-Daraqutni narrated from Ibn 'Umar that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Ash-shafaq is the redness; so when the twilight disappears, the prayer becomes due."

Al-Daraqutni said in "al-Gharayib": it is gharib (narrated through a single line), and all its narrators are trustworthy (thiqat). Ibn Khuzaymah also narrated in his "Sahih" from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, traced to the Prophet: "And the time of the Maghrib prayer lasts until the redness of the twilight departs," the hadith.

Ibn Khuzaymah said: If this wording is authentic, it suffices over other narrations; but Muhammad ibn Yazid alone narrated it.

Ibn Hajar said in "al-Talkhis": Muhammad ibn Yazid is al-Wasiti, and he is truthful (saduq). Ibn 'Asakir also narrated this hadith, and al-Bayhaqi regarded its stopping (waqf) at Ibn 'Umar as sound.

Al-Hakim also said that its traced form (raf') is an error. Indeed al-Bayhaqi said: this hadith has been narrated from 'Umar, 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit and Shaddad ibn Aws, and nothing in it is sound. But you know that the chain which Ibn Khuzaymah narrated in his "Sahih" contains nothing that necessitates its weakening except Muhammad ibn Yazid, and you know that he is truthful.

Among what indicates that the redness is the twilight is what al-Bayhaqi narrated in his "Sunan" from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, who said: "I am the most knowledgeable of people about the time of the 'Isha' prayer." He (ﷺ) used to pray it when the moon set on the third night (of the month). This is because a number of scholars have verified that the whiteness does not disappear until a third of the night has passed, and the moon sets on the third night of the month before that, as is well known.

* *

Al-Shawkani said in "Nayl al-Awtar": Among the proofs of those who say that ash-shafaq is the redness is what is narrated from him (ﷺ): "that he prayed 'Isha' when the moon set on the third night of the month." It was recorded by Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i.

Ibn al-'Arabi said: it is sound, and he prayed it before the disappearance of the twilight.

Ibn Sayyid al-Nas said in his "Sharh al-Tirmidhi": Everyone who has knowledge of the risings and settings (of the moon and stars) knows that the whiteness does not disappear until the first third of the night, and that is the limit which the Prophet (ﷺ) set for the exit from most of the time. Thus it is certain by the text that its time enters before the first third of the night with certainty. It has been established by the text that it enters before the disappearance of the twilight which is the whiteness; thus it becomes clear with certainty that the time enters with certainty by the twilight, which is the redness. End of quotation.

The beginning of the time of 'Isha' is the disappearance of the twilight by consensus, based on the hadith of Gabriel and the hadith of teaching, as mentioned earlier. This hadith and others are sufficient, and this is a clear proof that ash-shafaq is the redness and not the whiteness. In the "Qamus" (dictionary), ash-shafaq is the redness, and whiteness is not mentioned.

Al-Khalil, al-Farra' and others of the imams of the language said: ash-shafaq is the redness. What is narrated from Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, that ash-shafaq during travel is the redness, and during residence is the whiteness that follows the redness, does not contradict what we have mentioned, because it is a verification of the application (tahqiq al-manat) for the disappearance of the redness, which is the ash-shafaq according to Ahmad. Its explanation is that Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, says: "Ash-shafaq is the redness," and the traveller, because he is in the open desert and a spacious place, knows the setting of the redness. As for the one in residence, the horizon is hidden from him by walls, so he waits until the whiteness disappears in order to infer from its disappearance the setting of the redness. So his consideration of the disappearance of the whiteness is for its indication of the setting of the redness, not for itself. End of quotation from "al-Mughni" of Ibn Qudamah.

Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, and those who agree with him said: ash-shafaq is the whiteness that follows the redness. But you know that the verified view is that it is the redness. As for the last time of 'Isha', some sound narrations indicate that it ends at the first third of the night, some sound narrations say midnight, and some sound narrations indicate that it extends until dawn.

From the narrations that it ends at a third of the night is what al-Bukhari recorded in his "Sahih" from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "They used to pray 'Isha' between the disappearance of the twilight and the first third of the night."

In the hadith of Abu Musa and Buraydah mentioned earlier concerning the teaching of the one who asked about the times of prayer, in Muslim and others: "On the first night he (ﷺ) established 'Isha' when the twilight disappeared, and on the second night he delayed it until the first third of the night had passed. Then he said: The time is between these two."

In the hadith of Jabir and Ibn 'Abbas mentioned earlier concerning Gabriel leading in prayer: "On the first night he prayed 'Isha' when the twilight disappeared, and on the second night he prayed it when a first third of the night had passed, and said: The time is between these two times," and other narrations indicating that the time of 'Isha' ends when the first third of the night has passed.

From the narrations indicating that it extends to midnight is what the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) recorded in their two "Sahihs" from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) delayed 'Isha' until midnight, then prayed, then said: The people have prayed and slept, but you have been in prayer as long as you have been waiting for it." Anas said: "It is as if I am looking at the glint of his ring that night."

In the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr mentioned earlier, recorded by Ahmad, Muslim, al-Nasa'i and Abu Dawud: "And the time of the 'Isha' prayer is until midnight." In some of its narrations: "If you pray 'Isha', then its time lasts until midnight."

From the narrations indicating that it extends until the rising of dawn is what Abu Qatadah narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) in a long hadith, in which he said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no negligence in sleep; negligence is only upon the one who does not pray the prayer until the time of the next one comes." Recorded by Muslim in his "Sahih."

Know that the generality of this hadith is restricted by the consensus of the Muslims that the time of Subh does not extend after sunrise to the Zuhr prayer; so there is no time for Subh after sunrise by consensus. If it is said that the hadith of Abu Qatadah can be restricted by the hadiths indicating that the time of 'Isha' ends at midnight:

The answer: reconciliation (al-jam') is possible, and it is obligatory when possible, and applying both evidences is better than discarding one of them. The way of reconciling is that the limit at midnight is for the optional (ikhtiyari) time, and the extension until dawn is for the necessary (darurī) time.

What supports this is the unanimity of the scholars mentioned earlier that if a menstruating woman becomes pure one rak'ah before dawn, she prays Maghrib and 'Isha'. Those among the scholars who differed from what we mentioned earlier differed only concerning Maghrib, not concerning 'Isha'. Moreover, the report we presented earlier from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf and Ibn 'Abbas is not far from having the ruling of the traced (marfu') report, because a mawquf report in which opinion has no room has the ruling of a raised report, as established in the sciences of hadith. And it is known that the ending of the times of acts of worship, like their beginning, is not a matter for opinion, because it is purely devotional (ta'abbudi).

By this you know the way of reconciling what indicates that it ends at midnight and what indicates that it extends until dawn. But the difficulty remains between the narrations of the third and the narrations of the half. The apparent reconciliation, and Allah knows best, is that he made everything between the third and the half, which is a sixth, a container for the end of the optional time of 'Isha'.

Accordingly, its end has a beginning and an end, and this is the view of Ibn Surayj of the Shafi'is. And since this reconciliation in this way is not convincing, there is no way except to give preference among the narrations. Some scholars preferred the narrations of the third, because they are more cautious in preserving the preferred time, and because they are the subject of agreement, since the narrations agree that whoever prays 'Isha' before the third has performed his prayer within its optional time. Others preferred the narrations of the half, because they are an authentic addition, and the addition of a trustworthy narrator is accepted.

As for the beginning of the time of the Subh prayer, it is at the rising of the true dawn (al-fajr al-sadiq) by consensus of the Muslims, and it is the dawn which makes food and drink forbidden for the fasting person.

In the hadith of Abu Musa and Buraydah mentioned earlier in Muslim and others: "He commanded Bilal, and he established the dawn prayer when the dawn had broken, and people could hardly recognize one another," the hadith.

In the hadith of Jabir mentioned earlier, concerning Gabriel leading in prayer also: "Then he prayed Fajr when the dawn shone and food became forbidden for the fasting person." It is known that there are two dawns: the false (kadhib) and the true (sadiq). The false dawn does not make food forbidden to the fasting person, and the prayer of Subh is not valid with it; the true dawn is different in both respects.

As for the end of the time of the Subh prayer, some narrations limit it to the brightening (al-isfar), and some narrations indicate that it extends until sunrise. From the narrations indicating that it ends at the brightening is what is in the hadith of Jabir mentioned just above: "Then he came to him when it had become very bright, and said: Get up and pray it, and he prayed Fajr."

In the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas mentioned just before: "Then he prayed Subh when the earth had become bright," the hadith. This is in his explanation of the end of the preferred time of Subh on the second day.

In the hadith of Abu Musa and Buraydah mentioned earlier in Muslim and others: "Then on the next day he delayed Fajr until he finished from it while the speaker was saying: The sun has risen, or it nearly had."

From the narrations indicating that it extends until sunrise is what Muslim recorded in his "Sahih" and others from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr, may Allah be pleased with them both: "And the time of the Fajr prayer is as long as the sun has not risen."

In a narration of Muslim: "And the time of Fajr is as long as the first horn of the sun has not risen." The apparent way of reconciling these narrations is that the time ending at the brightening is the optional time of Subh, and the time extending until sunrise is its necessary time. This is the well-known position of Malik's school.

Some Malikis said: Subh has no necessary time; its entire time until sunrise is an optional time. According to this view, the way of reconciliation is what we mentioned earlier from Ibn Surayj concerning the end of the time of 'Isha'. And Allah knows best.

This, which we have mentioned, is the detailed explanation of the times, which was given in summary in the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, prayer has been decreed upon the believers a decree of specified times﴾ [4:103], and He clarified some of the explanation in His saying: ﴿Establish prayer at the decline of the sun﴾ [17:78], the verse,

• and His saying: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ [11:114], the verse.

and His saying: ﴿So glorify God when you enter the evening﴾ [al-Rum: 17], to the end of the verse.
And knowledge is with God, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 104:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not falter in pursuit of the enemy. If you are suffering pain, then indeed they suffer pain as you suffer pain, but you hope from Allah for what they do not hope for. And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise.﴾ (p-306) In this noble verse, Allah, exalted is He, forbids the Muslims from wahn (weakness, i.e., feebleness in pursuing their disbelieving enemies), and He informs them that if they feel pain from killing and wounding, then the disbelievers feel the same. The Muslim hopes from Allah for reward and mercy that the disbeliever does not hope for, so he is more deserving of patience over pains than they are. He clarified this meaning in several verses, such as His saying: ﴿And do not falter or grieve, and you will have the upper hand if you are believers﴾ and ﴿If a wound touches you, then a wound has already touched the people like it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 139–140], and such as His saying: ﴿So do not falter and call to peace while you have the upper hand, and Allah is with you and will not deprive you of your deeds﴾ [Muhammad: 35], and other verses besides these.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever earns a sin, he earns it only against himself﴾. In this verse He mentions that whoever commits a sin, the harm of it falls only upon his own self specifically and not upon anyone else. He clarifies this meaning in many verses, such as His saying: ﴿And every soul earns only against itself, and no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾ [al-An'am: 164], and His saying: ﴿And whoever does evil, it is against itself﴾ [Fussilat: 46], and other verses besides these.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 113:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He taught you what you did not know﴾ — the verse. In this noble verse He mentions that He taught His Prophet ﷺ what he did not know. In other places He makes clear that He taught him this through this Great Qur'an which He sent down to him, such as His saying: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a Spirit of Our command. You did not know what the Book was, nor [what] faith [was], but We made it a light, guiding thereby whom We will of Our servants﴾ — the verse [al-Shura: 52]; and His saying: ﴿We relate to you the best of stories in what We have revealed to you of this Qur'an, although before it you were among the unaware﴾ [Yusuf: 3], and other verses besides these.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 114:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk﴾, the verse, mentions in this noble verse that much of the private conversation of people among themselves contains no good.

In another place He forbade private conversation concerning what contains no good, and He explained that it is from Satan, to grieve the believers with it. This is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, when you confer privately, do not confer privately in sin and aggression and disobedience of the Messenger, but confer privately in righteousness and piety. And fear Allah, to whom you will be gathered.﴾ ﴿Secret conversation is only from Satan, that he might grieve those who have believed, but he cannot harm them at all, except by permission of Allah. And upon Allah let the believers rely.﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 10, 9].

His saying in this noble verse: ﴿or reconciliation between people﴾, does not clarify here whether by "people" is meant the Muslims to the exclusion of the disbelievers or not.

(p-307) However, he indicated in other places that what is meant by "people" in the case of reconciliation urged here is specifically the Muslims, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The believers are but brothers, so make reconciliation between your brothers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 10], and His saying: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight, then make reconciliation between them﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9]. His specifying the believers by mention indicates that others are not so, as is apparent. And like His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So fear Allah and set right your relations among yourselves﴾ [8].

Some scholars said: the enjoining of good mentioned in this verse, in His saying: ﴿except for one who enjoins charity or what is good﴾ [an-Nisa': 114], is clarified by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿By time, indeed, mankind is in loss, except for those who have believed and done righteous deeds and advised each other to truth and advised each other to patience﴾ [al-'Asr: 1, 2, 3], and His saying: ﴿except one whom the Most Merciful has permitted and who speaks correctly﴾ [an-Naba': 38]. The last verse is about the Hereafter, whereas the enjoining of good mentioned is only in this world. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 117:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they invoke none but a rebellious devil﴾. What is meant in this verse by their invoking the rebellious devil is their worship of him. Its parallel is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Did I not charge you, O children of Adam, that you should not worship Satan﴾ (the verse) [Ya-Sin: 60]; and His saying, addressing his friend Ibrahim in admonition to him: ﴿O my father, do not worship Satan﴾ [Maryam: 44]; and His saying, concerning the angels: ﴿Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾ (the verse) [Saba': 41]; and His saying: ﴿And thus their partners have made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children﴾ [al-An'am: 137]. These verses do not explain the manner of their worship of Satan, but He has explained in other verses that the meaning of their worship of Satan is their obedience to him, their following of his legislation, and their preferring it over what the Messengers brought from Allah, may He be exalted. An example is His saying: ﴿And indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you; and if you obey them, indeed you would be associating others with Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 121]; and His saying: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 31]. For ʿAdiyy ibn Hatim, may Allah be pleased with him, when he said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "How did they take them as lords?" the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "They made lawful for them what Allah had made unlawful, and made unlawful for them what Allah had made lawful, and they followed them," and that is the meaning of their taking them as lords. It is understood from these verses, with clarity admitting no ambiguity, that whoever follows the legislation of Satan, preferring it over what the Messengers brought, is a disbeliever in Allah, a worshipper of Satan, one who has taken Satan as a lord, even if he names his following of Satan by whatever names he wishes; for realities do not change by applying names to them, as is well known.

(p. 308) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And he said, "I will surely take from among Your servants an appointed portion"﴾. Here, in what is reported about Satan, He clarifies how he takes this appointed portion, through His saying: ﴿"And I will mislead them, and I will arouse in them desires, and I will order them so they will slit the ears of cattle, and I will order them so they will alter the creation of Allah"﴾ [al-Nisa, 119]. By slitting the ears of cattle is meant, for example, slitting the ear of a bahirah (a she-camel released after bearing a certain number of young, marked as sacred) and cutting it, so that this becomes a mark and sign that it is a bahirah or a sa'ibah (a freely released animal), as said by Qatadah, al-Suddi and others. Allah has nullified this practice through His saying: ﴿"Allah did not ordain any bahirah"﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Ma'idah, 103]. The meaning of "its ear being slit" is the slitting of its ear, as we have mentioned.

Al-tabtik (cutting, severing) in the language means cutting into pieces, and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

*Until, when the hand of the youth struck it down, it flew off, and in his hand were shreds of its feathers (bitak).*

That is, pieces. He also clarified how Satan takes this appointed portion in other verses:

• Like His saying: ﴿"I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path. Then I will surely come to them from before them and from behind them and from their right and from their left, and You will not find most of them grateful"﴾ [al-A'raf, 16].

• And His saying: ﴿"Tell me, this one whom You have honored over me; if You delay me until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely seize control of his descendants, except a few"﴾, to the end of the verse [al-Isra', 62]. Here it is not clarified whether the assumption Iblis made about the children of Adam, that he would take from them an appointed portion and that he would mislead them, came true for Iblis or not. But He clarified in another verse that his assumption did come true for him, which is His saying: ﴿"And Iblis had confirmed his assumption about them, so they followed him, except for a party of believers"﴾, to the end of the verse [Saba', 20]. Here it is not clarified which group is safe from being part of Iblis's portion, but He clarified it in other places:

• Like His saying: ﴿"I will surely mislead them all, except Your sincere servants among them"﴾ [al-Hijr, 39–40].

• And His saying: ﴿"His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and those who associate others with Him"﴾ [al-Nahl, 100], and other verses. Here it is not clarified whether this portion of Iblis is the majority or not, but He clarified in other places that it is the majority:

• Like His saying: ﴿"But most of the people do not believe"﴾ [al-Ra'd, 1].

• And His saying: ﴿"And most of the people, even if you strive, will not be believers"﴾ [Yusuf, 103].

• And His saying: ﴿"And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you"﴾ [al-An'am, 116].

• And His saying: ﴿"And certainly most of the former peoples had strayed before them"﴾ [al-Saffat, 71].

It is established in the Sahih that the share of Paradise is one out of a thousand, and the rest are in the Fire.

The Qur'an, verse 4:119: ﴿And I will surely command them, and they will surely alter the creation of Allah﴾

Some scholars said: The meaning of this verse is that Satan commands them to disbelief and to altering the natural disposition (fitrah) of Islam in which Allah created them. This interpretation is clarified and supported by His saying: ﴿So direct your face toward the religion, inclining to truth, the natural disposition of Allah upon which He created mankind. No change should there be in the creation of Allah﴾ [Ar-Rum: 30]. The meaning, in verification, is: Do not alter the natural disposition of Allah with which He created you, through disbelief. As for His saying, ﴿No change should there be in the creation of Allah﴾, it is a statement in the form of a report but intended as a command, signifying that it should only be complied with, as if it were a statement that will certainly occur. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿So there shall be no obscenity or disobedience﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 197], meaning: Do not commit obscenity, and do not commit disobedience. This is supported by what is established in the two Sahih collections (Sahihayn) from the hadith of Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Every child is born upon the fitrah. Then his parents make him a Jew, or a Christian, or a Magian, just as an animal gives birth to a complete animal. Do you find in it any mutilation?" And what Muslim narrated in his Sahih from Iyad ibn Himar ibn Abi Himar al-Tamimi, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed I created My servants as hanifs (upright in faith), then the devils came to them and led them astray from their religion and made unlawful for them what I had made lawful for them."

As for the view that the meaning of altering the creation of Allah in the verse is the castration of animals, and the view that it means tattooing, then the verse mentioned does not explain them. Groups of scholars held each of the mentioned views. The interpretation of some scholars that this verse refers to the castration of animals indicates that it is impermissible, because it is cited in the context of blame and of following the legislation of Satan. As for the castration of human beings, it is unanimously (ijma') forbidden, because it is mutilation, torture, cutting off a limb, and cutting off progeny without a legitimate reason, and it is not hidden that this is forbidden.

As for the castration of animals, a group of scholars permitted it when the benefit intended is either fattening or something else. The majority of scholars hold that there is no harm in sacrificing a castrated animal, and some considered it preferable if it is fatter than others. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz permitted the castration of horses, and Urwah ibn al-Zubair castrated a mule of his. Malik permitted the castration of male sheep. This is permissible because it is not done for the purpose of drawing closer to other than Allah, but only for the purpose of improving the flesh of what is eaten and strengthening the male when his desire for the female has ceased. Some of them disliked it, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Only those who do not know do that." This was stated by al-Qurtubi, and Ibn al-Mundhir chose it, saying: Because that is established from Ibn Umar, and he used to say: It is the growth of Allah's creation. Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan disliked it.

Al-Awza'i said: They used to dislike the castration of every animal that has offspring.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: On this topic there are two hadiths:

The first: From Ibn Umar, that the Prophet (ﷺ) "forbade the castration of sheep, cattle, camels and horses."

The second: The hadith of Ibn Abbas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) "forbade the mutilation of living creatures (sabr al-ruh) and the castration of animals."

What is found in the Muwatta' on this subject is what he mentioned from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, that he used to dislike castration and would say: In it is the completion of creation.

Abu Umar said, meaning in abandoning castration: the completion of creation. It is also narrated as: the growth of creation.

Al-Qurtubi said, after relating the statement which we have mentioned: I say: Abu Muhammad Abd al-Ghani has transmitted, from the hadith of Umar ibn Isma'il, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: "Do not castrate that which causes the creation of Allah to grow." It was narrated to him by al-Daraqutni, whose teacher said: Abbas ibn Muhammad narrated to us, Qurad narrated to us, Abu Malik al-Nakha'i narrated to us, from Umar ibn Isma'il, and he mentioned it.

Al-Daraqutni said: And it was narrated by Abd al-Samad ibn al-Nu'man from Abu Malik. End of quotation from al-Qurtubi in his own words. Likewise, according to the view that the meaning of altering the creation of Allah is tattooing, this also indicates that tattooing is forbidden.

It is established in the Sahih from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: Allah has cursed the women who tattoo and those who have themselves tattooed, the women who pluck their facial hair and those who have it plucked, and the women who file their teeth for beauty, who alter the creation of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Then he said: Shall I not curse the one whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed, and who is in the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic? Meaning His saying: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, refrain from it﴾ [Al-Hashr: 7].

A group of scholars said: The meaning of altering the creation of Allah in this verse is that Allah, exalted is He, created the sun, the moon, stones, fire and other created things for contemplation and for benefit, but the disbelievers altered them by making them deities to be worshipped.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah, exalted is He, created livestock to be ridden and eaten, but they prohibited them for themselves, and He made the sun, the moon and stones subservient to people, but they made them deities that they worship. Thus they altered what Allah had created.

As for what is narrated from Tawus, may Allah have mercy on him, that he would not attend the marriage of a black woman to a white man, or of a white woman to a black man, and he would say: This is from the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So they will surely alter the creation of Allah﴾ [Ibrahim: 119], this is rejected, because although the wording may allow it, the Sunnah has shown that it is not intended by the verse. Among that is the Prophet's (ﷺ) approval of the marriage of his freed slave Zayd ibn Harithah, may Allah be pleased with him, who was black, to Barakah, the mother of Usamah, who was an Abyssinian black woman, and among that is his (ﷺ) arranging the marriage of Usamah ibn Zayd to Fatimah bint Qays, who was a fair-skinned Qurashi woman, while Usamah was black. And Bilal's wife was the sister of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf of the Banu Zuhrah ibn Kilab. Tawus, may Allah have mercy on him, despite his knowledge and eminence, erred in this matter.

The author of this commentary, may Allah pardon him, says: Similar to Tawus's view on this verse is what some scholars of the Maliki school said: that a black woman may be married off by the general authority of the Muslims, based on the premise that Malik permits the marrying off of a woman of lower standing by general authority, a Muslim, if she has no specific guardian who can compel the marriage. They said: A black woman is of lower standing absolutely, because blackness is a defect in creation. This view is rejected by the scholars who are verifiers (muhaqqiqin). The truth is that a black woman may be noble, and may be beautiful. Some poets have said:

A black-skinned woman shows you a face upon which the water of bliss has flowed.
My eye saw her and went towards her, for the likeness of a thing is attracted to it.

Another said:

I have an Abyssinian woman who has captivated my heart, and my soul does not yearn for anyone other than her.
It is as if her qualities are three paths along which souls travel towards their desire.

Another said about a black woman:

Musk resembled you, and you resembled it, standing in its color, sitting.
There is no doubt, since your color is one, that you are both of one clay.

Similar examples in the speech of the poets are numerous.

His saying: ﴿And I will surely command them, and they will surely cut the ears of cattle﴾ [An-Nisa: 119] indicates that cutting the ears of cattle is not permissible, and this is so. As for cutting the ear of the bahirah and the sa'ibah in drawing nearer to idols, this is unanimously disbelief in Allah. As for cutting the ears of animals for other than that, it is apparently also impermissible. For this reason, the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded us: "to look for the eye and the ear (for soundness), and not to sacrifice one that is one-eyed, nor one with a cut ear from the front, nor one with a cut ear from the back, nor one with a split ear, nor one with a bored ear." Narrated by Ahmad, the authors of the four Sunan, al-Bazzar, Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, and al-Bayhaqi, from the hadith of Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and al-Tirmidhi authenticated it, while al-Daraqutni declared it defective (a'allahu). Al-Muqabalah is the one whose ear tip is cut off, al-Mudabarah is the one whose back of the ear is cut off, al-Sharqa' is the one whose ear is split lengthwise, and al-Kharqa' is the one whose ear has been pierced with a round hole. Thus, the defect in the ear is considered by the majority of scholars.

Malik and al-Laith said: An animal whose ear is cut off is not acceptable, or most of its ear is cut off; this was stated by al-Qurtubi. The well-known position of the Maliki school is that what prevents acceptability is cutting off a third of the ear or more, not less, so it does no harm. And if it is a sakka', which is one born without an ear, Malik and al-Shafi'i said: It is not acceptable. If its ear is small, it is acceptable. The same is narrated from Abu Hanifah. If it is split for the branding mark, it is acceptable according to al-Shafi'i and the majority of jurists. This was stated by al-Qurtubi in his commentary on this verse. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 4, verse 123:
